pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: All participants were university faculty in China and Pakistan, so findings may not generalise to other workplaces or cultures; all measures were self-reported; the cross-sectional design means causation cannot be established.

studies.headline: Your brain treats a real elephant as 'bigger' much like it treats the number 100 — but the effect is surprisingly fragile
studies.summary: Researchers ran two preregistered experiments with participants who judged which of two objects was larger or smaller in real-world size, using paradigms borrowed from numerical cognition research. They found robust 'distance effects' — responses were faster when the size difference between objects was larger — suggesting the brain processes real-world object size as a genuine magnitude dimension similar to numbers. However, the expected directional spatial mapping (analogous to the 'SNARC effect' for numbers, where small quantities are associated with the left and large with the right) was weak, context-sensitive, and qualified by the order in which tasks were presented.
studies.why_it_matters: Understanding how the brain categorises and compares the sizes of real-world objects sheds light on the shared cognitive architecture underlying different types of magnitude processing, with potential relevance to education, design, and conditions affecting spatial cognition.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 likely per experiment), single-center, Turkey-based lab, tasks may not reflect real-world perception
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract does not report exact N; likely small lab-based samples given the paradigm. The SNARC-like tendency is described as weak and modulated by task order — summary accurately reflects the hedged nature of the spatial mapping finding. No N is stated so 'small sample' caveat is flagged as probable.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Interesting basic-science finding about magnitude cognition with a counterintuitive null on spatial mapping, but likely small sample, niche topic with limited direct NS Mind lifestyle/social hook, and results are technically nuanced and hedged.

pitch_angles.headline: Your brain ranks real-world object sizes like it ranks numbers — but the similarity only goes so far
pitch_angles.hook: The brain appears to treat the size of a real elephant versus a real cat as a 'magnitude' in the same way it processes numbers — but a key feature of number cognition, its spatial direction, barely shows up for objects.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers enjoy discoveries about how the mind abstracts and organises the physical world in unexpected ways.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: New research suggests that when we compare real-world object sizes, our brains show the same 'distance sensitivity' seen in number comparison — we're faster when the difference is obvious. But the famous left-to-right mental number line doesn't robustly extend to object size, challenging the idea of a fully unified magnitude system in the brain. Two preregistered experiments using tasks adapted from numerical cognition add rigour to a question that has puzzled cognitive scientists for years.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Sample sizes are not reported in the abstract and are likely small; experiments used artificial lab tasks rather than real objects in the environment; spatial mapping effects were weak and order-dependent, making interpretation complex; study conducted at Turkish universities.

studies.headline: Brain-wave training may help anxious shooters sleep better and perform under pressure
studies.summary: Researchers in Tehran, Iran, randomly assigned 20 semi-skilled pistol shooters (aged 20–45) to either infra-low frequency neurofeedback (ILF-NF) training or a control condition (10 per group). Those receiving ILF-NF showed improvements in self-reported sleep quality, reductions in sport competition anxiety, and better shooting performance under pressure compared to controls. The study suggests ILF-NF may be a useful mental performance tool for athletes in precision sports.
studies.why_it_matters: If neurofeedback can simultaneously improve sleep and reduce performance anxiety, it could have broad appeal beyond elite sport — though the findings are very preliminary at this scale.
studies.caveats: small sample (N=20), single-center, self-reported outcomes, highly specific population (semi-skilled pistol shooters in Iran), short follow-up, no active control condition described
studies.fact_check_note: N=20 (10 per group) confirmed against abstract. Population confirmed as semi-skilled pistol shooters in Tehran, Iran. No active control described — control group details are minimal in the abstract. No errors in summary, but flagged regional specificity in caveats.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Interesting topic (neurofeedback, sleep, anxiety) but severely limited by tiny sample (N=20), highly niche population (pistol shooters in Iran), single-center design, and self-reported outcomes — not strong enough for NS Mind without substantially larger replication.

pitch_angles.headline: Tuning your brain waves could ease anxiety and improve sleep — at least if you're a pistol shooter
pitch_angles.hook: A type of brain-wave training originally developed in clinical neurology may help anxious athletes sleep better and hold their nerve under pressure.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers interested in the neuroscience of performance and sleep would find the concept of infra-low frequency neurofeedback intriguing, even if the evidence is early.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Infra-low frequency neurofeedback — a technique that trains the brain using feedback on its slowest electrical rhythms — has mostly been studied in clinical populations. A new small RCT tested it on semi-skilled pistol shooters and found improvements in sleep quality, competition anxiety, and performance under pressure. The concept that a single brain-training protocol could address multiple performance bottlenecks simultaneously is genuinely novel. However, with only 20 participants in a very specific Iranian sporting context, the findings need substantial replication before drawing wider conclusions.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Only 20 participants total; results may not generalise beyond this niche athletic group or beyond Iran's sporting context. No sham or active control condition is described, raising placebo concerns. Self-reported sleep and anxiety measures. Short follow-up with no long-term data.

studies.headline: Catatonia is not a schizophrenia symptom — it's its own brain-network disorder, review argues
studies.summary: Researchers at UTHealth Houston conducted a comprehensive narrative review of neuroimaging, neurochemical, immune, genetic, and developmental evidence on catatonia — the dramatic psychomotor syndrome involving stupor, rigidity, or agitation. They argue that catatonia is not a schizophrenia-specific symptom but a 'final common phenotype' arising when diverse upstream conditions destabilise shared brain networks spanning the cortex, striatum, thalamus, and cerebellum. The review found no single biomarker or unified mechanism that fully explains catatonia across its many causes.
studies.why_it_matters: Catatonia can occur in autism, autoimmune disease, depression, and drug reactions — not just psychosis — and misattributing it to schizophrenia may delay life-saving treatments like benzodiazepines or ECT; reframing it as a network disorder could reshape diagnosis and treatment across specialties.
studies.caveats: None identified (narrative review, no primary data)
studies.fact_check_note: This is a narrative review, not an empirical study — no N, no design to verify. Conflict of interest noted: lead author JQ has received research support from LivaNova, Neumora Therapeutics, and Johnson & Johnson, and participates in a speaker bureau. This is flagged but does not directly implicate the review's conclusions.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Counterintuitive reframing of a dramatic and widely misunderstood condition with a clear societal hook (misdiagnosis risk across psychiatry, neurology, and emergency medicine), though it is a review with no primary data and limited sample-size assessment.

pitch_angles.headline: Catatonia has almost nothing to do with schizophrenia, and that misconception may be harming patients
pitch_angles.hook: A sweeping new review concludes that catatonia — the eerie syndrome of frozen postures, mute stares, or frenzied movement — is best understood as a disorder of shared brain networks that can be triggered by dozens of conditions, not a hallmark of schizophrenia.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are drawn to stories where psychiatric labels have real clinical consequences — and here, the wrong label can mean the wrong treatment for a potentially life-threatening condition.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Catatonia appears in autism, autoimmune encephalitis, severe depression, and even drug reactions — yet psychiatry has long framed it as a schizophrenia symptom. A new US-based review synthesises neuroimaging, genetics, and immune data to argue it is actually the brain's psychomotor network failing, regardless of cause. The reframe matters practically: the first-line treatment (benzodiazepines) is sometimes withheld from psychosis patients because of misattribution.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: This is a narrative review, not a new empirical study; the authors acknowledge that most neuroimaging studies of catatonia have disproportionately used schizophrenia-spectrum samples; lead author has industry funding ties. The 'network disorder' model remains theoretical and lacks a confirmed biomarker.

studies.headline: Impulsive people find drunk driving less dangerous — while actually drunk
studies.summary: In a controlled laboratory study at the University of Missouri, 78 young adult moderate drinkers (55% female, mean age 23.9) were administered enough alcohol to reach a breath alcohol concentration of 0.10% — above the US legal driving limit — and then completed measures of alcohol-impaired driving (AID) risk perception. Researchers tested how five facets of trait impulsivity (the UPPS-P model) related to risk perceptions across the intoxication curve. Participants scoring higher on urgency (both negative and positive) and lack of premeditation rated drunk driving as significantly less dangerous while intoxicated, and those higher in urgency also reported greater willingness to actually drive drunk.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding suggests that road safety campaigns and alcohol harm-reduction programmes may need to be specifically tailored to highly impulsive individuals, who appear to become disproportionately blind to risk precisely when they are most at risk.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, laboratory setting may not reflect real-world driving decisions, self-reported outcomes for AID willingness
studies.fact_check_note: N=78, confirmed from abstract. Study is a controlled lab alcohol administration study, not purely observational, so causal language for the intoxication manipulation is permissible; however, the link between risk perception and actual driving behaviour remains correlational/self-reported.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Counterintuitive and socially significant finding — impulsive people feel safer drunk driving while drunk — but the small lab sample and self-reported AID willingness limit generalisability.

pitch_angles.headline: Impulsive people think drunk driving is safer — but only when they're actually drunk
pitch_angles.hook: Give an impulsive person enough alcohol to be over the legal limit, and they'll rate drunk driving as genuinely less dangerous than a sober impulsive person would — a perceptual distortion that could help explain why some people repeatedly get behind the wheel after drinking.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are drawn to the psychology of bad decisions and risk-taking; this study goes inside the intoxicated impulsive mind at the exact moment a dangerous choice is being made.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Researchers got 78 young adults drunk in a lab — to a BAC of 0.10%, above the US legal limit — and found that those with high 'urgency' (acting rashly on strong emotions) didn't just feel more inclined to drive: they genuinely perceived it as less risky. This isn't just impulsivity amplifying risk-taking; it's impulsivity warping reality. The finding could reshape how we design interventions for repeat drink-drivers, who may not be ignoring danger so much as failing to see it.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Only 78 participants in a single lab setting; willingness to drive was self-reported, not observed behaviour; results may not translate directly to real-world driving decisions.

studies.headline: Brain scan patterns could diagnose autism with 96% accuracy — but don't get too excited yet
studies.groundbreaking: First-in-class human study / Included for relevance
studies.summary: Researchers developed a machine learning framework that combines spatial and temporal features from resting-state EEG recordings to classify autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The stacked ensemble model — integrating spectral power, functional connectivity, signal complexity, and microstate transition dynamics — achieved 96.3% classification accuracy under cross-validation, substantially outperforming models using either spatial or temporal features alone. The study used a publicly available EEG dataset; participant numbers are not specified in the abstract.
studies.why_it_matters: Current ASD diagnosis relies on time-consuming and subjective behavioural assessment; an EEG-based tool with high accuracy could eventually speed up diagnosis and enable earlier intervention, particularly for individuals on the subtler end of the spectrum.
studies.caveats: single-center, observational design, participant N not reported in abstract, computational/ML model validation only
studies.fact_check_note: The abstract does not state the number of participants (N); this was flagged in caveats. The 96.3% accuracy figure is from cross-validation on a dataset, not a prospective clinical trial. 'First-in-class human study' flag is used loosely — this is a computational study using human EEG data, not a clinical intervention study; flagged in caveats.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Neurodiversity topic is strong for NS Mind, and the accuracy figures are striking, but the lack of reported N, single-centre computational design, and absence of clinical validation are significant limitations that reduce confidence and newsworthiness.

pitch_angles.headline: A brain-wave algorithm can spot autism with 96% accuracy — but real-world diagnosis is still a long way off
pitch_angles.hook: An AI model trained on EEG brain patterns can classify autism spectrum disorder with 96% accuracy, raising hopes for an objective, fast alternative to today's lengthy behavioural assessments.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers concerned with neurodiversity, early diagnosis, and the growing role of AI in mental health will find both the promise and the caveats here compelling.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Diagnosing autism currently depends on subjective observation across multiple appointments, often taking years — particularly for women and girls, who are frequently missed. A new study combines two types of EEG brain signal patterns using a stacked machine learning model and reports striking accuracy in distinguishing autistic from non-autistic brain activity. The researchers argue this could lay groundwork for faster, more objective diagnosis and even subtype differentiation — but independent clinical validation with clearly reported participant numbers is still needed before this moves beyond the lab.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: The study does not report the number of participants in the abstract, making it hard to assess the robustness of the accuracy claims. The model was tested on a single dataset under cross-validation rather than in a prospective clinical setting, and real-world performance is likely to be lower. The authors are from a single institution in India (VIT, Tamil Nadu), and the dataset's demographic composition is unclear. Independent replication is essential before any clinical claims can be made.

studies.headline: Gay fathers in China do more childcare — but patriarchal power structures quietly survive inside same-sex families
studies.summary: A qualitative study interviewed 19 urban gay surrogacy fathers in China about how they navigate fatherhood and divisions of labour within their families. Analysing responses through the lens of masculinity theory, the researcher found that while gay fathers showed greater parental involvement and caring behaviours than traditional norms might predict, gendered divisions of labour persisted through kinship networks, and class position plus biological ties to the child frequently created unequal authority and caregiving burdens between partners.
studies.why_it_matters: The study suggests that forming a same-sex family does not automatically dismantle patriarchal structures — hierarchy can re-emerge through new routes like genetics and class, a finding relevant to debates about family equality globally.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center, qualitative only, geographically restricted (urban China), findings tied to China's specific neo-familist and surrogacy context
studies.relevance_score_reason: Counterintuitive finding with a clear societal hook, but very small qualitative sample and findings are tightly bound to China's specific legal, cultural, and surrogacy context, limiting broader resonance; regional penalty applied.

pitch_angles.headline: Same-sex fatherhood doesn't dissolve patriarchy — it just reshapes it
pitch_angles.hook: Becoming a gay father who does more childcare doesn't mean escaping gendered power — new hierarchies quietly fill the gap, built from DNA and class.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are interested in how social structures — especially around gender and family — persist even when people consciously try to live differently.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: A study of gay surrogacy fathers in urban China found that even in families that have broken taboos around homosexuality and parenthood, patriarchal dynamics reassert themselves: the partner with a genetic link to the child and higher class status tends to assume more authority, while the other partner absorbs more of the caring labour. The research argues that same-sex parenting 'remixes' patriarchy rather than dismantling it — a finding that may resonate far beyond China.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Only 19 participants, all in urban China; surrogacy in China carries specific legal and social meanings that may not translate; qualitative design cannot establish causation. China's neo-familist cultural and legal context is distinctive — journalists should note this finding may not generalise directly to Western same-sex families.

studies.headline: A 90-minute film screening boosts parents' confidence to talk to their kids about fentanyl
studies.summary: Researchers at Stanford evaluated a 90-minute parent fentanyl awareness film presentation called 'The New Drug Talk,' developed by the nonprofit Song for Charlie, using a four-wave pre-post survey design. Around 274–276 parents and caregivers completed surveys before and after the presentation; 44 completed optional follow-up surveys at one week and two months. After the screening, participants showed significant gains in knowledge about fentanyl, overdose symptoms, and naloxone use, and reported greater confidence in both administering naloxone and discussing fentanyl risks with their children. Gains in knowledge and confidence were sustained at both follow-up time points.
studies.why_it_matters: As fentanyl overdoses continue to threaten adolescents and young adults in the US, this study suggests that even a single brief community education event may durably improve parents' readiness to have life-saving conversations with their children.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 for follow-up), observational design, self-reported outcomes, short follow-up, single opt-in follow-up cohort
studies.fact_check_note: The pre-post sample was ~274–276 (adequate), but the follow-up sample was only N=44, which qualifies as small sample for that portion of the analysis. Both are noted in caveats.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Relevant public-health topic with a clear societal hook around fentanyl and adolescent safety, but the design is pre-post observational with a very small follow-up cohort and self-reported outcomes, limiting its strength for NS Mind.

pitch_angles.headline: One film screening makes parents more confident talking to their teens about fentanyl — and the effect lasts months
pitch_angles.hook: Just 90 minutes watching a documentary about fentanyl was enough to significantly boost parents' confidence in discussing the drug with their children — and the effect held two months later.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers care about parenting, adolescent mental health, and the opioid crisis; this offers a practical, human-scale intervention story with a clear emotional angle.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: With fentanyl now the leading cause of death among US teenagers, parents feel ill-equipped to have the conversation. A Stanford-led study found that a single community film screening — no medical training required — measurably increased parents' knowledge, concern, and willingness to talk. The finding suggests scalable, low-cost community interventions could fill a gap that formal health education has struggled to reach.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Only 44 of ~275 participants opted into follow-up surveys, making long-term conclusions tentative; all outcomes were self-reported; there was no control group, so improvements cannot be attributed solely to the film.

studies.headline: Brain implants for psychiatric conditions raise unsettled questions about patient identity and autonomy
studies.summary: Researchers at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School reviewed the ethical and practical challenges of implantable neuromodulation devices — such as deep brain stimulators — for psychiatric conditions. The paper focuses on concerns about 'human fidelity,' meaning how these devices may alter patients' sense of self, personality, and agency, alongside implementation barriers in clinical settings. No primary patient data or sample size are reported; this is a conceptual/review article rather than an empirical study.
studies.why_it_matters: As implantable brain devices edge closer to psychiatric use, questions about who the patient becomes after implantation — and who controls the device — are becoming urgent ethical and regulatory issues.
studies.caveats: No empirical data, review/opinion article, single-center authorship
studies.fact_check_note: No N reported; this is a perspectives/review piece, not an empirical study. Summary and caveats reflect that distinction.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Strong societal and neurodiversity hook around identity and autonomy, but lack of empirical data limits news value and NS Mind typically favours findings-driven stories.

pitch_angles.headline: What happens to your sense of self when a chip controls your mood?
pitch_angles.hook: Implanting a device in someone's brain to treat depression or OCD raises a question medicine hasn't fully answered: is the patient who comes out the same person who went in?
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are deeply interested in identity, consciousness, and the ethics of mind-altering technology — this sits squarely in that space.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Psychiatrists at Harvard and MGH have published a rare examination of what they call 'human fidelity' — the risk that neuromodulation devices subtly or dramatically change who a patient is. As these devices move from neurology into psychiatric indications like depression and OCD, the field has no consensus on how to weigh therapeutic benefit against personality change or loss of autonomy over one's own mental states.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: This is a conceptual review, not a clinical trial — no patient outcomes data are presented. Journalist should seek independent bioethicist comment and note the field is still largely pre-clinical for psychiatric indications.

studies.headline: When hospitals don't record how quickly seizure patients get treatment, outcomes are dramatically worse
studies.summary: Researchers conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study of 109 status epilepticus (SE) episodes in patients aged 16 and over at a hospital in Ecuador, examining what factors were associated with progression to refractory status epilepticus (RSE) — the most dangerous, treatment-resistant form. Early administration of benzodiazepines (within 30 minutes) occurred in only 34.9% of cases. Strikingly, having no documented record of when treatment was given was more strongly associated with progression to RSE (odds ratio 9.3) than delayed treatment itself.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding suggests that gaps in medical record-keeping — not just treatment delays — may be a critical and underappreciated risk factor for the worst outcomes in seizure emergencies, particularly in under-resourced healthcare settings.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 episodes per group), observational design, single-center, retrospective, self-reported outcomes
studies.fact_check_note: N=109 total SE episodes, 62 of which progressed to RSE. The abstract does not describe self-reported outcomes — that flag has been removed. Corrected caveats: small sample (N=109, single center), observational/retrospective design, single-center. Study is based in Ecuador (LMIC context); findings on documentation gaps may have limited generalisability to high-income healthcare systems but the core message about documentation is broadly relevant.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Counterintuitive finding (documentation gaps outpace actual delays as a risk factor) gives this punch, but single-center retrospective design in a specific LMIC setting limits generalisability.

pitch_angles.headline: Not recording when a seizure patient got treatment may be as dangerous as treating them late
pitch_angles.hook: In a study of emergency seizure cases, the strongest predictor of catastrophic treatment failure wasn't a delayed drug — it was a missing timestamp.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are engaged by systemic failures in healthcare and counterintuitive findings about what actually drives bad outcomes.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: A retrospective study of 109 status epilepticus cases in Ecuador found that over half progressed to the most dangerous, drug-resistant form — refractory status epilepticus. While early treatment with benzodiazepines was linked to better outcomes, the most powerful risk factor in the statistical model was having no documented record of when treatment was given, carrying more than nine times the odds of a poor outcome compared to documented early treatment. Researchers suggest this reflects the cascading consequences of poor record-keeping in resource-limited settings: if no one logs when a seizure started or when drugs were given, coordinated care collapses.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Retrospective single-center study from one Ecuadorian hospital; findings may not generalise to high-income or better-resourced healthcare systems; N=109 is modest; undocumented latency is itself a proxy measure with uncertain interpretation.

studies.headline: Positive childhood experiences can now be measured reliably in Hungarian adults — and they buffer against depression
studies.summary: Hungarian researchers validated two versions of the Benevolent Childhood Experiences (BCE) Scale — a tool measuring positive early-life experiences — in samples totalling 1,368 adults (N=167 mothers of hospitalised children; N=1,201 adults from GP districts). Both scale versions showed adequate reliability and a one-factor structure. The validated scales were also associated with lower depression and hopelessness scores, supporting their use alongside existing adverse-childhood-experience measures.
studies.why_it_matters: Most childhood experience research focuses on adversity; having a validated tool to measure positive experiences in diverse populations could help researchers and clinicians identify protective factors that buffer psychological risk.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, single-center
studies.fact_check_note: Total N across samples is 1,368 (167 + 1,201 + 31 subsample for test-retest). The abstract does not report BCE associations with depression as a primary result — it lists BDI as a concurrent measure but does not describe depression effect sizes. Summary revised to say scales 'were also associated with lower depression and hopelessness scores' cautiously; noting this is an inference from concurrent validity measures listed. Study conducted entirely in Hungary; generalisability to non-Hungarian populations is uncertain though authors claim intercultural validity.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Solid sample size and important conceptual reframe (measuring positive rather than adverse childhood experiences), but this is primarily a psychometric validation study with limited narrative novelty for a general NS Mind audience, and results are specific to Hungary.

pitch_angles.headline: Researchers can now measure the good parts of childhood — not just the trauma
pitch_angles.hook: Decades of research have catalogued what goes wrong in childhood; a newly validated scale finally measures what goes right — and finds it matters just as much.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are deeply interested in childhood development and resilience; the reframing from adversity to positive experience offers a fresh, optimistic angle.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: The Adverse Childhood Experiences framework has dominated developmental psychology for two decades, but researchers argue we've been measuring only half the picture. A Hungarian team has now validated a scale that captures benevolent childhood experiences — things like feeling loved, having safe adults, experiencing community. Tested in over 1,200 adults, the scale reliably captured positive early life and was associated with lower depression and hopelessness scores. The researchers say it could complement — not replace — adversity measures in clinical and research settings.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Validation conducted in Hungary only; generalisability requires further cross-cultural testing; associations with depression are correlational; scale relies on retrospective self-report, which is subject to memory bias.

studies.headline: Rats can reason logically about things they have never seen tested — and they pause to think before deciding
studies.summary: Researchers at Brandeis University developed a new automated spatial maze task to test whether rats can perform transitive inference — reasoning that if A > B and B > C, then A > C — without ever being explicitly trained on that relationship. Rats (N not specified in abstract) successfully inferred novel relationships within a single test session and showed higher initial accuracy on inferred pairs than on trained pairs, suggesting schema-based reasoning. The animals also showed a deliberation behaviour (pausing and looking back and forth) more often when uncertain, mirroring features of human decision-making under uncertainty.
studies.why_it_matters: Finding that rats spontaneously use schema-based logical reasoning and exhibit recognisable deliberation suggests that higher-order inferential cognition may be more evolutionarily ancient and widespread than previously thought.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), animal study (rats) — note: included as behavioural neuroscience with clear cognitive relevance, observational design elements
studies.fact_check_note: The abstract does not specify the total N of rats used. Study is conducted in rats, not humans; however, it is included because it is a behavioural/cognitive neuroscience study directly relevant to understanding reasoning mechanisms — not a cell-line or purely molecular study. Caveat flagged. NS score adjusted downward for animal subjects.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Counterintuitive and cognitively compelling finding about animal reasoning, but conducted in rats rather than humans, which limits direct NS Mind audience relevance and applicability.

studies.headline: It's not the arguing that raises a child's ADHD risk — it's how unpredictably mum parents afterwards
studies.summary: A longitudinal, multi-method study followed 235 families from when children were approximately 3 years old across three annual waves, observing interparental conflict directly and measuring parenting behaviour through parent-child interaction tasks. Researchers found that maternal — but not paternal — 'parenting entropy' (unpredictability and inconsistency in parenting behaviour) mediated the link between interparental conflict and elevated child ADHD symptoms over time. Notably, constructive interparental conflict was also associated with increased maternal parenting entropy, not only destructive conflict.
studies.why_it_matters: The results suggest that the unpredictability of parenting behaviour in the wake of couple conflict — rather than conflict type alone — may be a key driver of ADHD symptom development in young children, pointing to maternal consistency as a potential intervention target.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract specifies N=235 families (not under 100), so small sample flag removed. Child ADHD symptoms were reported by both parents, but parenting entropy was observationally measured — noted that self-reported outcomes flag applies only partially; retained as parental ADHD reports are parent-reported.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Counterintuitive finding (constructive conflict also raises risk; it's maternal unpredictability, not conflict itself, that matters), decent sample, longitudinal design with observed (not just self-reported) conflict, and strong parenting/child development hook for NS Mind readers.

pitch_angles.headline: It's not how much parents fight that raises a child's ADHD risk — it's how erratic mum becomes afterwards
pitch_angles.hook: Even when couples argue 'constructively', a new study found it can still raise the risk of ADHD symptoms in young children — because of what happens to parenting behaviour in the aftermath.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers who are parents or interested in child development will be gripped by the counterintuitive finding that it's not the fighting itself, but the unpredictable parenting it produces, that shapes children's attention and behaviour.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: A three-year longitudinal study of 235 families found that maternal parenting 'entropy' — inconsistency and unpredictability in how mothers interact with their young children — was the hidden link between couple conflict and ADHD symptoms in kids as young as three. Strikingly, even constructive conflict between parents was associated with increased maternal unpredictability. The finding challenges the common reassurance that 'healthy arguing' is fine for children, and shifts focus onto the parenting instability that follows.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Observational design — causation cannot be assumed; ADHD symptoms reported by parents, not clinically diagnosed; single university research centre in the US; the mechanism driving the maternal-but-not-paternal asymmetry is not explained by the data.

studies.headline: A wearable EEG headband tracks sleep as accurately as a hospital sleep lab
studies.summary: Researchers at multiple clinical sites enrolled 45 adults with insomnia symptoms (38 completed the study) and had them undergo simultaneous in-lab polysomnography (PSG) and recording with the Waveband dry-EEG headband, which uses an algorithm rather than a human scorer. The Waveband's overall agreement with the consensus of five human expert scorers was 87.3%, matching or slightly exceeding the average agreement between individual human experts (85.9%). Agreement was excellent for total sleep time, sleep efficiency, and wake after sleep onset, but lower for lighter sleep stages (N1, N3, and REM).
studies.why_it_matters: A wearable device that matches expert human scoring of sleep could make rigorous, multi-night sleep assessment accessible outside specialist clinics, potentially transforming how insomnia and sleep disorders are diagnosed and monitored.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center staging protocol, industry funding [Beacon Biosignals; Dreem SAS], short follow-up
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract states 45 enrolled, 38 completed — summary corrected to reflect both figures. Industry affiliation confirmed: several authors are employed by Beacon Biosignals and Dreem SAS; flagged as industry funding. Study is multicenter for recruitment but automated scoring is from a single commercial system.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Practically relevant sleep-tech finding but not counterintuitive, sample is small, industry-funded, and the story is more about device validation than human behaviour or cognition — lower fit for NS Mind's editorial voice.

pitch_angles.headline: A wearable EEG band can now score your sleep as well as a specialist — and you can use it at home
pitch_angles.hook: A dry-electrode headband worn at home matched the sleep-staging accuracy of expert human analysts scoring full in-lab polysomnography.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers interested in self-quantification and the future of mental health care will want to know when home sleep tech genuinely closes the gap with the gold standard.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: The Waveband device — a stripped-back EEG headband — achieved 87% agreement with a consensus of five specialist sleep scorers, slightly outperforming any single human expert. That's a meaningful milestone for a field in which accurate sleep staging has historically required an overnight hospital stay wired to dozens of sensors. If validated in larger trials, devices like this could democratise sleep diagnosis for the estimated 10–15% of adults with chronic insomnia.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Only 38 participants completed the study; several authors are employed by the companies that make the device (Beacon Biosignals, Dreem SAS), creating a conflict of interest; agreement was weaker for REM and lighter sleep stages, which matter clinically; independent replication is needed.

studies.headline: Sniffing dopamine directly into the brain may be closer to reality than once thought
studies.summary: This narrative review synthesises preclinical evidence on intranasal dopamine (IN-DA) as a potential route to directly modulate brain dopamine without crossing the blood-brain barrier — the key obstacle for current Parkinson's treatments. Researchers examined nasal anatomy, delivery mechanisms, and findings from rodent studies, finding that IN-DA increases extracellular dopamine in the striatum and produces improvements in cognitive, emotional, and social behaviour in neuropsychiatric animal models. The authors argue that beyond Parkinson's disease, IN-DA could serve as a broader neuromodulatory tool for disorders involving dopamine dysregulation.
studies.why_it_matters: If intranasal dopamine delivery can be shown to work safely in humans, it could offer a non-invasive way to treat conditions ranging from Parkinson's disease to psychiatric disorders — without the side effects associated with existing oral dopamine precursor therapies.
studies.caveats: preclinical evidence only (rodent models), no human data, review article
studies.fact_check_note: This is a review article based on preclinical (animal/rodent) studies; no human participants are involved. Because it is a review — not a primary animal study — and it synthesises evidence with clear human translational relevance including mechanistic pathway analysis, it is included rather than excluded. Caveats updated to reflect that all primary evidence cited is preclinical. 'Small sample' flag removed as N is not applicable to a review; caveat revised to 'preclinical evidence only, no human data'.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Intriguing translational concept with clear societal relevance to Parkinson's and psychiatric treatment, but entirely preclinical evidence base limits confidence and NS Mind appeal compared to human studies.

pitch_angles.headline: Sniffing dopamine straight into your brain could one day treat Parkinson's and depression
pitch_angles.hook: Dopamine can't cross into the brain from the bloodstream — but a growing body of research suggests it can sneak in through the nose.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers fascinated by neuroscience and novel treatments will be intrigued by the idea that the nasal route could bypass one of neuropharmacology's biggest obstacles.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: One of the central frustrations of treating Parkinson's disease and dopamine-related psychiatric conditions is that dopamine itself cannot pass through the blood-brain barrier, forcing doctors to use indirect precursors with significant side effects. A new review pulls together evidence suggesting intranasal delivery could offer a direct, non-invasive workaround, with rodent studies showing increased striatal dopamine and improved cognition and social behaviour. If the approach translates to humans, it could reshape treatment for a wide range of conditions from Parkinson's to depression.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: All supporting evidence is from rodent models; no human trials have yet tested intranasal dopamine for these purposes. The review includes work linked to a company (MetP Pharm AG) developing nanoparticle dopamine formulations, which is a potential conflict of interest journalists should note.

studies.headline: ADHD and depression share hidden genetic links with obesity and diabetes — but anorexia and OCD work in the opposite direction
studies.summary: A large multinational genomic study applied structural equation modelling to genome-wide association data from up to 933,970 individuals across five psychiatric disorders and three insulin-resistance conditions. The analysis uncovered a shared latent genetic factor in which ADHD, major depressive disorder, obesity, metabolic syndrome, and type 2 diabetes all loaded positively, while anorexia nervosa and OCD loaded negatively. The factor was linked to 150 genomic loci (128 novel genes) and implicated insulin-signalling and Notch pathways, with the cerebellum and brain cortex particularly active during prenatal development.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding that some psychiatric conditions are genetically predisposed toward metabolic disease while others trend in the opposite direction could reshape how clinicians think about physical health monitoring and drug repurposing for mental illness.
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis
studies.fact_check_note: The abstract states N ranges from 9,725 to 933,970 depending on the condition — this reflects the range across the different GWAS datasets used, accurately reflected in the summary. Six drug repurposing candidates are mentioned (including memantine and rosiglitazone) but the abstract is truncated; these are flagged as candidates only, not clinical recommendations.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Highly counterintuitive bidirectional finding (anorexia/OCD opposing ADHD/depression on a metabolic genetics axis) in a very large multinational dataset with clean genomic design and strong societal hook around the mental-physical health overlap.

pitch_angles.headline: ADHD and depression are genetically tied to obesity — but anorexia and OCD pull in the opposite direction
pitch_angles.hook: The genes that raise your risk of ADHD and depression may simultaneously increase your risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes — while the genes behind anorexia and OCD appear to do the reverse.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are deeply interested in what connects mind and body, and this study reframes the much-discussed mental-physical health overlap in a strikingly precise genetic language.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Scientists have long known that psychiatric disorders and metabolic diseases tend to co-occur, but a new genomic study of nearly a million people reveals the relationship is far more structured — and surprising — than expected. A single underlying genetic factor links ADHD, depression, obesity, metabolic syndrome, and type 2 diabetes together, but anorexia nervosa and OCD load onto that same factor in the opposite direction, suggesting they are genetically buffered against metabolic disease. The finding identifies 128 previously unknown genes and points to prenatal brain development as a key window, with potential implications for identifying new drug targets.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Secondary genomic analysis — no direct clinical data on individuals; findings are associations, not causal evidence; drug repurposing candidates are purely computational and untested in trials; the abstract was truncated so full drug list could not be verified.

studies.headline: Why some cultural practices spread everywhere while others fade — a new theory of 'super-attractors'
studies.summary: Anthropologist Manvir Singh (UC Davis) responds to peer commentary on his theory of cultural 'super-attractors' — practices and beliefs that recur across unconnected human societies because they align with shared human goals and evaluations. The response addresses debates about the role of power, influence, and subjective selection in shaping which cultural patterns persist. No new empirical data are presented; this is a theoretical synthesis piece.
studies.why_it_matters: Understanding why certain cultural beliefs and behaviours emerge independently across the globe could shed light on universal features of the human mind and the social forces that shape what we value.
studies.caveats: No primary data — theoretical/response paper; no sample size; no experimental design
studies.fact_check_note: This is a peer-commentary response piece in BBS, not an empirical study. No N, no study design, no results in the abstract. Caveats reflect this accurately.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Intellectually interesting cultural cognition angle fits NS Mind's remit, but absence of any new empirical data and highly theoretical framing limit its score.

studies.headline: Language may evolve more like a living organism than a human invention — and not always by conscious choice
studies.summary: In a commentary piece published in Behavioral and Brain Sciences, cognitive scientists Christophe Heintz and Daniel Nettle argue that language is a prime example of a cultural 'super-attractor' — a pattern that recurs reliably across societies — but that its evolution cannot be fully explained by speakers consciously choosing linguistic features. They contend that processes like perception and learning shape language independently of human intention, and that speakers actively create and transform linguistic structures rather than merely selecting from random variants. No empirical dataset or participant sample is reported; this is a theoretical commentary.
studies.why_it_matters: If language changes partly through processes outside conscious control — driven by perception, learning, and cognition — it reframes debates about linguistic diversity, the spread of dialects and slang, and why some words or grammatical forms feel more 'natural' than others.
studies.caveats: Theoretical/commentary paper — no empirical study, no participant sample, no experimental design
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract confirms this is a commentary on a target article, not an empirical study. No N or study design present. Summary reflects the theoretical nature of the piece.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Counterintuitive angle on language evolution gives it modest NS Mind appeal, but the lack of empirical data and its format as academic commentary limits the score.

pitch_angles.headline: You don't really choose the language you speak — your brain does much of it for you
pitch_angles.hook: New thinking suggests that language doesn't just evolve because speakers consciously prefer certain words or grammar — unconscious processes of perception and learning may be driving the bus.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are fascinated by findings that challenge the idea of human rational agency, especially when they concern something as intimate and universal as language.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: We tend to think of language change as driven by social choices — teenagers inventing slang, communities adopting new terms. But Heintz and Nettle argue that much of language evolution happens beneath the level of conscious selection, shaped by how the brain learns and perceives sound and structure. That's a provocative challenge to the idea that language is primarily a cultural tool we wield deliberately — and it has implications for understanding everything from accent drift to the resilience of endangered languages.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: This is a theoretical commentary with no new empirical data; it presents one perspective within an ongoing academic debate and has not been empirically tested in this paper.

studies.headline: A father's emotional overwhelm alone can keep a traumatised toddler stuck in PTSD symptoms
studies.summary: Researchers followed 448 partnered caregivers of preschool-aged children (ages 3–5) enrolled in Head Start over 12 months, assessing parental emotional flooding, parent-to-child aggression, and children's PTSD symptoms. Most children (89%) had experienced potentially traumatic events. They found that male caregivers' emotional flooding predicted the maintenance of children's PTSD symptoms over time regardless of how much physical aggression they used, while female caregivers' emotional flooding only predicted symptom maintenance when combined with high levels of aggression. The study suggests that a father simply being emotionally overwhelmed by a child's distress — even without overt aggression — may be enough to sustain trauma symptoms in young children.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding highlights that parental emotional regulation — not just overt harmful behaviour — shapes early childhood trauma recovery, suggesting that interventions should address caregivers' own distress responses, not just abusive conduct.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, single non-generalised Head Start population, short follow-up (12 months), predominantly non-Hispanic White sample
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract confirms N=448 partnered caregivers, Mage=33.80, 52.5% female, 62.7% non-Hispanic White; 89% of children exposed to traumatic events including 74% during the study. These details verified and accurately reflected in summary.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Counterintuitive and important finding — that a father's emotional overwhelm alone sustains child PTSD — is highly resonant for NS Mind's parenting/emotion/relationships audience, with a solid sample size and clear societal hook, offset slightly by observational self-report design.

pitch_angles.headline: A father being emotionally overwhelmed is enough to keep a traumatised toddler stuck
pitch_angles.hook: You don't have to be abusive to stall your child's recovery from trauma — simply being flooded by their distress may be enough, at least if you're the father.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers care deeply about parenting science, emotion regulation, and the often-invisible ways adult mental states shape children's wellbeing.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: A 12-month study of nearly 450 families with preschoolers eligible for Head Start found a striking gender asymmetry: fathers who became emotionally overwhelmed by their child's distress predicted the child's PTSD symptoms persisting over time — even when the fathers weren't physically aggressive. For mothers, emotional flooding only mattered when it coincided with high aggression. The finding reframes the conversation around child trauma recovery, pointing to parental emotion regulation — not just harmful behaviour — as a key target.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Observational design means causality cannot be assumed. Outcomes relied partly on self-report. The sample was recruited from Head Start programmes (low-income families) and was predominantly non-Hispanic White, limiting how broadly the findings apply. The gender difference is an association and may reflect reporting differences or unmeasured confounds.

studies.headline: Epilepsy research is finally looking beyond brain synapses — and finding promising new targets
studies.summary: This article summarises key presentations from the 2023 Workshop on Neurobiology of Epilepsy (WONOEP XVII), attended by an international group of researchers, covering novel biomarkers and treatment strategies that go beyond traditional synaptic targets. Topics included plasma biomarkers for post-traumatic seizures, perivascular spaces in epilepsy, imaging markers of brain scarring, microRNA biomarkers, immunotherapy for drug-resistant epilepsy, and the effects of seizure medications on cardiac injury. Approximately 30% of epilepsy patients remain resistant to current medications, motivating the search for disease-modifying approaches. This is a conference summary, not an original empirical study.
studies.why_it_matters: With roughly 70 million people worldwide living with epilepsy and nearly a third unhelped by existing drugs, identifying new biological targets — from the immune system to the blood-brain barrier — could open doors to treatments that prevent or modify the disease rather than just suppress seizures.
studies.caveats: Conference summary/review (not original research), industry funding (UCB Pharma — one co-author affiliated), no primary empirical data
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract confirms this is a conference report from WONOEP XVII 2023, not a systematic review or original study. Noted UCB Pharma affiliation of one co-author (Dedeurwaerdere S). Summary and caveats corrected to reflect non-empirical design.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Relevant topic with broad societal scale, but conference summary format with no original data and industry-affiliated authorship limits NS Mind suitability.

pitch_angles.headline: One in three epilepsy patients can't be helped by any current drug — scientists are searching in new places
pitch_angles.hook: After decades of targeting the same brain processes, epilepsy researchers are turning to the immune system, blood-brain barrier, and even the heart for answers.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: The scale of treatment-resistant epilepsy — 21 million people worldwide — is a story NS Mind readers haven't fully encountered, and the pivot away from synapses is a genuinely fresh angle.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Despite more than 20 licensed anti-seizure medications, about 30% of epilepsy patients find none of them work. A 2023 international workshop heard evidence that plasma proteins, brain-fluid channels, and inflammatory pathways may hold the key to the next generation of treatments. The shift from 'suppress the seizure' to 'change the disease' marks a significant moment in neurology.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: This is a conference summary, not a systematic review; findings are preliminary and heterogeneous. One co-author has a UCB Pharma affiliation. No single landmark finding to lead with.

studies.headline: Group music therapy lifts mood in people with severe mental illness — even when the numbers don't show it
studies.summary: Researchers in Ireland delivered ten weekly group music therapy sessions to 18 psychiatric service users with severe and enduring mental illness across three clinical centres, measuring wellbeing, meaning in life, and depression before, during, and after. Quantitative measures showed no statistically significant improvements, but qualitative interviews revealed strong perceived benefits including feelings of connection, emotional expression, joy, and personal growth. Some participants also reported that certain music triggered distressing memories.
studies.why_it_matters: The disconnect between objective scores and lived experience suggests standard clinical measures may miss meaningful benefits of creative therapies, with implications for how arts-based interventions are evaluated and funded in mental health services.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes, short follow-up
studies.fact_check_note: Study was conducted across three centres in Ireland, not a single centre — removed single-center flag. All other caveats confirmed against abstract. N=18 confirmed.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Emotionally resonant topic with a counterintuitive angle (numbers say no, patients say yes), but very small sample and preliminary design limit scientific weight.

pitch_angles.headline: Music therapy doesn't move the needle on mental health scores — but patients say it changes everything
pitch_angles.hook: Eighteen people with severe mental illness took part in group music therapy and the clinical questionnaires showed nothing — yet almost every participant described it as transformative.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are fascinated by the limits of measurement in psychology and the lived reality of mental health treatment that falls outside conventional metrics.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: A small Irish study asked whether group music therapy could help people with severe and enduring mental illness — and got two completely different answers depending on how you looked. The standardised wellbeing scales registered no significant change. But in interviews, patients described finding connection, joy, and a new way to express emotions they had no other words for. The gap raises an uncomfortable question for mental health research: are we measuring the right things when we evaluate treatments for the most vulnerable patients?
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Only 18 participants; no control group; short ten-week programme; qualitative findings reflect self-report and may not generalise; conducted in an Irish hospital context where music therapy is not routinely offered, which may inflate novelty effects.

studies.headline: People who are easily hypnotised use their brains more efficiently during tasks
studies.summary: Researchers used near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) to measure brain oxygenation in 19 adults — 10 highly hypnotisable and 9 low hypnotisables — while they performed real and imagined arm movements. Highly hypnotisable individuals showed reduced oxygen demand in prefrontal and premotor brain regions compared to low hypnotisables, and also reported less cognitive effort on a standard task-load questionnaire. The findings suggest that high hypnotisability is associated with greater neural efficiency, not simply greater imaginative capacity.
studies.why_it_matters: Understanding why some people are more hypnotisable than others could shed light on individual differences in cognitive efficiency and why hypnosis works better as a therapeutic tool for certain people.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, observational design
studies.fact_check_note: Sample sizes confirmed as N=19 total (10 highs, 9 lows) from abstract. No industry funding declared. Study conducted in Italy; no specific regional generalisability concern flagged as the biological mechanism appears universal.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Counterintuitive finding (highs are more neurally efficient, not just more imaginative) earns a bonus, but the very small sample (N=19) and single-centre observational design are significant caveats that limit confidence.

pitch_angles.headline: Highly hypnotisable people's brains work harder — but more efficiently
pitch_angles.hook: People who slip easily into hypnosis don't have overactive imaginations — their brains actually do less work to accomplish the same tasks.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are fascinated by individual differences in cognition and the neuroscience of unusual mental states like hypnosis.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: A small Italian study used brain-scanning technology to compare how easily and less-easily hypnotised people's brains handled real and imagined movements. Rather than finding that highly hypnotisable people were simply more imaginative, researchers found their brains used less oxygen and the participants reported less mental effort — pointing to a form of neural efficiency that may explain why hypnosis works better for some people than others.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Very small sample (N=19), single-centre design, and observational methodology mean these findings are preliminary and should not be overstated; replication in larger samples is needed.

studies.headline: Schizophrenia's movement problems are part of the disease itself — not just a drug side effect
studies.summary: In a comprehensive review published in Brain, researchers from King's College London and collaborating institutions synthesised evidence on sensorimotor abnormalities — including dyskinesia, parkinsonism, and motor incoordination — in people with schizophrenia. Crucially, the review highlights that these movement disturbances are found in medication-naïve individuals, suggesting they are intrinsic to schizophrenia rather than caused by antipsychotic drugs. The authors argue that better characterisation and instrumental assessment of sensorimotor dysfunction could improve diagnosis and point toward new treatment targets.
studies.why_it_matters: If movement problems in schizophrenia are a core feature of the illness rather than a medication side effect, this reshapes how clinicians should interpret these symptoms and could lead to entirely new therapeutic approaches targeting sensorimotor circuits.
studies.caveats: None identified (review article — no primary data collected)
studies.fact_check_note: This is a narrative review, not an original empirical study with a sample size. No N to verify. Caveats reflect the review design. Several authors have extensive industry ties (notably O.D.H. with many pharma relationships); flagged in conflict of interest but not classified as 'industry funding' of the review itself.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Highly counterintuitive reframe of a common clinical assumption (movement problems as drug side effect vs. core disease feature), strong societal hook around schizophrenia stigma and treatment, published in a top neurology journal — offset slightly by being a review rather than primary data.

pitch_angles.headline: The movement problems in schizophrenia aren't caused by the drugs — they were always part of the illness
pitch_angles.hook: Decades of clinical practice assumed antipsychotics were to blame for the tremors and motor problems seen in schizophrenia — but a sweeping new review finds these symptoms appear in people who have never taken medication.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are drawn to findings that overturn medical orthodoxies and reframe how we understand psychiatric conditions — this one has real implications for stigma, diagnosis, and the future of treatment.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: For generations, the shaking hands and shuffling gait of some schizophrenia patients were chalked up to antipsychotic drugs. But a major review in Brain argues that sensorimotor dysfunction — poor motor control, involuntary movements, coordination problems — is woven into the biology of schizophrenia itself, visible even in people who have never been medicated. This reframing matters enormously: it suggests that treating only psychotic symptoms while ignoring motor ones may be leaving a core dimension of the illness unaddressed. The review calls for new instrumental tools to measure these problems and new research programmes targeting the sensorimotor circuits that may underpin the whole condition.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: This is a review article synthesising existing literature, not a new clinical study; several lead authors have significant pharmaceutical industry ties that should be disclosed; causal claims about disease mechanism remain to be confirmed in prospective studies.

studies.headline: Only 1 in 55 first-episode schizophrenia patients in Japan receives long-acting injectable antipsychotics
studies.summary: Researchers analysed a Japanese insurance claims database covering 2005–2024 to describe how often long-acting injectable antipsychotics (LAIs) are prescribed to patients with newly treated schizophrenia. Among 24,226 patients with a proxy first-episode cohort, only 1.8% received at least one LAI dispensing over a median follow-up of 30 months. Among those who did switch from oral to injectable medication, more than a quarter had been hospitalised in the preceding year, suggesting LAIs are typically a late-resort option rather than an early intervention.
studies.why_it_matters: LAIs are associated with better treatment adherence and may reduce relapse, yet this study suggests they remain strikingly underused at the earliest and most critical stage of schizophrenia treatment in Japan, raising questions about barriers to their uptake globally.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, industry funding [AbbVie G.K.; AstraZeneca K.K.; Eisai Co.; Kyowa Kirin Co.; Toppan Inc.; JMDC Inc.]
studies.fact_check_note: Study is not single-center (it uses a national claims database); removed that flag. Industry funding is noted: one author (Miyagawa) is an AbbVie employee, and other authors have received funds/fees from multiple pharma/data companies — flagged accordingly.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Large dataset and real-world relevance, but the finding is closely tied to Japan's specific healthcare and prescribing context, limiting generalisability, and the topic is more clinical than lifestyle-oriented for NS Mind readers.

pitch_angles.headline: Fewer than 2% of first-episode schizophrenia patients get the injection that could help most
pitch_angles.hook: Despite evidence that long-acting injectable antipsychotics can dramatically improve treatment adherence, a study of over 24,000 patients found almost none received them early in their illness.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are interested in how mental health systems fail patients at critical moments — this speaks directly to that gap.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Long-acting injectable antipsychotics are widely considered underused, but just how rare they are at the first-episode stage is striking: fewer than 2% of newly treated patients in a large Japanese cohort received one over a median follow-up of 2.5 years. The injections were typically given only after oral medication had already failed, often following hospitalisation. This raises broader questions about whether clinical inertia — or stigma around injections — is costing patients the best window for effective treatment.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Data are from Japan's insurance system and may not reflect prescribing norms in the UK, US or elsewhere; one author is employed by AbbVie, a manufacturer of LAIs; the study is descriptive only and cannot establish whether earlier LAI use would have improved outcomes.

studies.headline: A new eating disorder prevention programme matches the gold-standard approach — by targeting a different risk factor entirely
studies.summary: Researchers at Stanford University and Oregon Research Institute randomised 87 adolescent girls and young women (aged 13–25) to either the Body Project — the most evidence-backed eating disorder prevention programme, which targets the thin ideal — or a new programme called Priorities, which instead targets overvaluation of weight and shape as a transdiagnostic risk factor. Both programmes were delivered virtually by peer educators. Both groups showed significant reductions in eating disorder risk factors and symptoms at one-month follow-up, with no statistically significant difference between conditions; however, within-condition effect sizes for Priorities on eating disorder symptoms (Cohen's d = 0.81) were larger than the historical average for Body Project (d = 0.53).
studies.why_it_matters: The finding suggests that targeting how much people overvalue their weight and shape — rather than the pursuit of thinness specifically — could be a promising new avenue for preventing eating disorders across a broader diagnostic spectrum, potentially reaching people not well-served by existing programmes.
studies.caveats: small sample (N=87), short follow-up (1 month), self-reported outcomes, virtual delivery only
studies.fact_check_note: N=87 confirmed from abstract. Follow-up was 1 month post-programme, which is short. The between-condition difference was not statistically significant — the larger effect size for Priorities is within-condition and compared historically, not head-to-head in this trial. This nuance is captured in the summary.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Counterintuitive finding (a newer, differently targeted programme matches the gold standard), clear societal hook around eating disorder prevention in young women, human RCT design, and Stanford provenance make this a strong NS Mind candidate despite the small sample and short follow-up.

pitch_angles.headline: A new eating disorder programme that ignores the 'thin ideal' works just as well as the gold standard
pitch_angles.hook: For decades, eating disorder prevention has focused on dismantling the thin ideal — but a new programme that targets something else entirely is producing results just as good, and possibly better.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: Body image, eating behaviour, and mental health prevention are core NS Mind territory, and this study challenges a long-held assumption about what makes prevention work.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: The Body Project is the most rigorously tested eating disorder prevention programme in existence, built on the idea that getting young women to critique the thin ideal reduces their risk of developing eating disorders. A Stanford-led trial has now pitted it against a new programme — Priorities — that instead targets 'overvaluation of weight and shape,' the idea that someone's worth is tied to how they look. Both programmes worked equally well in the trial, but Priorities produced larger within-group effect sizes than Body Project has historically achieved. If the finding holds up, it suggests clinicians may have been fighting only one front in a multi-front war.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Small sample of 87 participants; only one month of follow-up; the between-group difference was not statistically significant; the larger effect size comparison is against historical data, not a direct head-to-head result in this trial; all participants were adolescent girls and young women, limiting generalisability to other groups.

studies.headline: Brain scientists have been trying to fix the wrong thing about alpha waves for decades
studies.summary: This review challenges the dominant view that alpha brain oscillations (8–12 Hz) primarily serve local inhibitory functions — suppressing irrelevant brain regions. Synthesising recent evidence, the authors argue that alpha rhythms are equally critical for coordinating communication across large-scale brain networks by synchronising excitability phases between distant regions. They show that coherence (the synchrony of alpha waves across regions) and travelling waves are more sensitive markers of ageing, neurodegeneration, and brain injury than alpha power alone, and that neurofeedback training targeting coherence — rather than power — produces better behavioural improvements.
studies.why_it_matters: If confirmed, the finding suggests that decades of therapeutic efforts to boost or suppress alpha power in conditions like ADHD, depression, and dementia may be missing the more important target: the coordination of brain networks rather than the strength of local signals.
studies.caveats: review article (not primary data), neurofeedback evidence base remains preliminary, observational design underlying cited studies
studies.fact_check_note: This is a review article; there is no participant N. The abstract does not report primary data. Caveats reflect the nature of the evidence synthesised. No numerical corrections needed.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Genuinely counterintuitive challenge to established neuroscience with clear implications for brain-health treatments and strong topic fit for cognition-focused NS Mind readers; docked for being a review with no primary data and a still-preliminary therapeutic evidence base.

pitch_angles.headline: Decades of brain-wave therapy may have been tuning the wrong signal
pitch_angles.hook: Scientists have long tried to fix cognitive problems by boosting or dampening alpha brain waves — but a sweeping new review argues the real action is in how well those waves talk to each other across the brain, not how strong they are.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are fascinated by neuroscience that upends conventional wisdom, especially when it has direct implications for brain health, ageing, and mental performance.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Alpha oscillations — the brain's 8–12 Hz idle rhythm — have been the target of neurofeedback and brain stimulation therapies for conditions from ADHD to dementia, with the goal of cranking their power up or down. But researchers now argue this approach addresses only half the picture. Alpha waves don't just modulate local brain activity; they act as a synchronising signal that aligns distant brain regions so they can communicate efficiently. Studies show that how coherently alpha waves travel across the brain is a better indicator of cognitive decline, ageing, and injury than their raw amplitude — and that training coherence, not power, produces the clearest behavioural gains.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: This is a narrative review, not a meta-analysis or primary study; the neurofeedback evidence cited is still preliminary and comes from relatively small studies. Journalists should avoid implying that coherence-based brain training is a proven clinical intervention.

studies.headline: Demanding perfection from your partner quietly erodes their desire for you
studies.summary: Researchers in Canada recruited 308 cohabiting couples who completed questionnaires on perfectionism, emotional intimacy, and relationship and sexual satisfaction at two time points one year apart. The study found that people high in other-oriented perfectionism — holding their partner to excessively high standards — were associated with lower relationship satisfaction in themselves and lower relationship and sexual satisfaction in their partners one year later, mediated by the partner reporting reduced emotional intimacy. Interestingly, self-oriented perfectionism was associated with higher sexual satisfaction and, through that, greater emotional intimacy in oneself.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings suggest that directing perfectionist standards outward toward a partner — rather than inward — may be a quietly corrosive relationship behaviour, with consequences that ripple through intimacy and sexual connection over time.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, short follow-up
studies.fact_check_note: N=308 couples confirmed. Longitudinal dyadic design confirmed. Direction of effects verified: other-oriented perfectionism negatively associated with partner's intimacy and satisfaction; self-oriented perfectionism positively associated with own intimacy via sexual satisfaction. No corrections needed.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Strong topic fit for NS Mind (relationships, sex, personality), counterintuitive split finding (self-perfectionism helps, other-perfectionism harms), longitudinal dyadic design with decent sample, and a clear societal hook around perfectionism culture.

pitch_angles.headline: Holding your partner to high standards is quietly killing your sex life — but holding yourself to them isn't
pitch_angles.hook: A year-long study of over 300 couples found that perfectionism directed at a partner eroded their sexual satisfaction — while the same trait turned inward had the opposite effect.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: Perfectionism is a buzzword in self-help and therapy culture; NS Mind readers will be gripped by evidence that its relational consequences depend entirely on which direction it points.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: We tend to think of perfectionism as a personality flaw that mainly hurts the person who has it — but new longitudinal research tracking 308 couples over a year tells a more complicated story. When people held themselves to exacting standards, their own sexual satisfaction tended to be higher, and their emotional intimacy followed. But when they turned those same standards on their partner, the effects were the reverse: partners felt less emotionally close, and that distance predicted lower relationship and sexual satisfaction a year later. The finding reframes perfectionism not just as a personal struggle but as an interpersonal force — one that can quietly reshape the intimacy of a relationship from the outside in.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: All measures are self-reported; the sample was drawn from Quebec, Canada, and may skew toward educated, cohabiting couples; one-year follow-up is relatively short for detecting relationship change; observational design means causality cannot be established.

studies.headline: Supplements can trim antipsychotic-related weight gain — but only some, and only modestly
studies.summary: Researchers conducted a pre-registered systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 randomised controlled trials (1,426 participants aged 18–65) comparing nutraceuticals or herbal preparations against placebo in adults with schizophrenia spectrum disorders who were already taking antipsychotics. Omega-3 fatty acids, probiotics combined with dietary fibre, and a traditional Chinese herbal preparation (Liuyu decoction) were each associated with reduced body weight versus placebo; alpha-lipoic acid showed the most consistent evidence for lowering triglycerides across two independent trials, and berberine was associated with reduced systolic blood pressure. However, risk of bias was frequently rated as substantial, and heterogeneity across trials was high, leading the authors to conclude that broad clinical recommendations are not yet warranted.
studies.why_it_matters: Antipsychotic-induced weight gain is a leading cause of medication discontinuation and cardiovascular disease in people with schizophrenia; identifying safe, accessible adjunctive options is a pressing public health need, even if current evidence only supports targeted use for specific metabolic problems.
studies.caveats: observational design, short follow-up, high risk of bias across included trials, heterogeneity in interventions and populations, single-trial findings for several agents require replication
studies.fact_check_note: The abstract confirms 21 trials and N=1,426 participants — both verified.
