'Single-center' flag added as all groups were recruited by the same Polish research team across affiliated institutions. No industry funding declared.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Strong societal hook around aggression and rehabilitation, and the brevity of the intervention is counterintuitive, but the very small N, lack of control group, and mixed results across subgroups significantly limit the story.

pitch_angles.headline: Three therapy sessions may be enough to stop people assuming the worst in others
pitch_angles.hook: Just three meetings — six sessions — of a talking-based therapy appears to reduce the hair-trigger tendency to read hostility into other people's faces and actions, even in juvenile offenders.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are deeply interested in the malleability of social cognition and whether short, accessible psychological interventions can genuinely shift entrenched patterns of thought.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Hostile attribution bias — the reflexive assumption that others mean harm — is a well-established driver of aggression and conflict. A new pilot study tested whether a brief, three-meeting mentalization module could dent that bias in some of the hardest-to-reach populations: inmates and juvenile offenders. The finding that it showed measurable shifts, at least in some groups and on some tasks, raises a provocative question about how little therapeutic input might be needed to begin reshaping social perception.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Only 58 participants across four very different groups; no randomised control condition; effects were inconsistent across subgroups and task types; results should be considered preliminary and hypothesis-generating only.

studies.headline: A surprisingly small amount of exercise eases premenstrual symptoms — but doesn't change how women cope
studies.summary: Brazilian researchers assigned 33 university students with premenstrual syndrome (PMS) to either an 8-week minimum-dose resistance training protocol or a control condition involving only physical testing. Psychological PMS symptoms were measured using the Premenstrual Symptom Screening Tool (PSST) and coping strategies with the Brief COPE, analysed via linear mixed models. The resistance training group showed significant reductions in psychological PMS symptoms compared to controls. However, no changes in coping strategies were observed in either group, suggesting that exercise and coping style operate through independent pathways.
studies.why_it_matters: PMS affects up to 47% of people who menstruate, and the finding that even a minimum-dose exercise protocol may reduce symptoms offers a low-barrier, accessible option — though the absence of any effect on coping strategies suggests exercise alone is unlikely to address all dimensions of PMS.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center, short follow-up
studies.fact_check_note: The study is described as 'nonrandomized' in the title, which is a meaningful design limitation not captured by the original input tags. Added 'observational design' to caveats accordingly. N=33 confirmed from abstract.

pitch_angles.headline: Even a bare minimum exercise routine reduces PMS symptoms — but it won't change how you cope
pitch_angles.hook: Just eight weeks of low-dose resistance training was enough to reduce psychological premenstrual symptoms — but it did nothing to alter the coping strategies women used to manage them.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are interested in accessible, evidence-based lifestyle interventions for mental health, and this study delivers a nuanced message about what exercise can and cannot do.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: The idea that you need a rigorous, sustained exercise regime to see mental health benefits has become almost axiomatic — but a small Brazilian trial found that a deliberately minimal resistance training protocol was sufficient to reduce PMS-related psychological symptoms in just two months. The catch? It had no effect whatsoever on how participants coped with stress, suggesting that exercise and psychological coping are separate levers. For the millions of people who menstruate and struggle with PMS each month, the result is both encouraging and a useful corrective against overclaiming what exercise can fix.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Non-randomised design means group differences at baseline cannot be ruled out. Only 33 participants from a single Brazilian university, so findings may not generalise. Short follow-up means nothing is known about whether benefits persist beyond eight weeks.

studies.headline: A brain signal pattern may finally tell doctors whether an epilepsy implant is working — in real time
studies.summary: Researchers prospectively enrolled 11 patients with drug-resistant epilepsy who were receiving deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT), then retrospectively analysed the effects of stimulation on local field potential (LFP) recordings captured via an implanted Medtronic Percept device. The study found that suppression of slow gamma oscillations (20–50 Hz) in the ANT — a signal pattern the authors term 'gamma fade' — was associated with long-term seizure reduction: six of seven patients exhibiting these oscillations were treatment responders (defined as achieving more than 50% seizure frequency reduction). Notably, only one of the six responders was still using the standard clinical stimulation parameters at final follow-up, suggesting that the standard settings may not be optimal for all patients.
studies.why_it_matters: Currently, clinicians have no real-time way to judge whether DBS settings are working in drug-resistant epilepsy patients — they must wait months for seizure diaries to accumulate; a validated biomarker could make personalised, faster-adjusting treatment possible for one of the hardest-to-treat neurological conditions.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, observational design, short follow-up, self-reported outcomes (seizure diary)
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract confirms N=11 total, with seven exhibiting the relevant oscillations and six of those being responders. The retrospective analysis within a prospective trial is noted. No corrections needed to the direction of findings; 'gamma fade' terminology is used in the abstract. Self-reported seizure diary confirmed as the outcome measure.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Strong real-world significance and a first-in-class biomarker angle (+2 counterintuitive, +1 societal hook) in a human study, but the very small N=11 and multiple methodological caveats substantially limit confidence in the findings (−3 across small N, single-center, self-report).

pitch_angles.headline: A fading brain wave pattern could finally tell doctors if an epilepsy brain implant is actually working
pitch_angles.hook: Right now, doctors fitting epilepsy patients with brain stimulators have to wait months and rely on patient diaries to know if the device is helping — but a newly identified brain signal may change that.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers interested in neurotechnology, personalised medicine, and the hidden complexity of treating the brain will be gripped by the idea that a simple oscillation pattern could unlock truly adaptive brain implants.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: For people with drug-resistant epilepsy, deep brain stimulation offers hope — but it comes with a frustrating blind spot: doctors set the parameters largely by guesswork and wait months to see results. A small but striking new study suggests that a specific pattern of electrical activity in the thalamus, a gradual quieting of 'slow gamma' waves dubbed 'gamma fade', tracks closely with whether patients actually stop having seizures. Even more surprising, when researchers tested multiple stimulation settings in clinic, they found that most responding patients were not best served by the standard textbook parameters. The finding points toward a future where implants adjust themselves in real time, guided by the brain's own feedback signals.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: The study included only 11 patients at a single centre, outcomes relied on self-reported seizure diaries, and the analysis was retrospective within a prospective trial — results must be treated as preliminary until replicated in larger, multi-site cohorts.

studies.headline: Hidden depression and anxiety — not just aggression — are driving young people back into the justice system
studies.summary: This narrative review synthesised evidence from multiple countries on the role of internalising mental health disorders — including depression, anxiety, PTSD, self-harm, and suicidal behaviour — in juvenile offending and reoffending. Rather than focusing on the externalising or aggressive behaviours typically associated with youth crime, the review found that untreated inward distress is associated with higher rates of reoffending, worse life outcomes, and elevated suicide risk among justice-involved youth. The review also summarised promising interventions, including cognitive behavioural therapy, family-based approaches, mindfulness, and mentoring, noting that these show potential for reducing both symptoms and recidivism. The authors highlight especially severe gaps in low- and middle-income countries, where stigma and resource shortages leave most affected youth without any mental health support.
studies.why_it_matters: Juvenile justice systems worldwide tend to focus on punishment or externalising behaviour; this review suggests that failing to screen and treat depression, anxiety, and trauma in young offenders may be actively fuelling reoffending and suicide risk.
studies.caveats: observational design
studies.fact_check_note: This is a narrative review, not an empirical study with a participant N — no sample size flag is applicable. Caveat updated accordingly to reflect the review methodology rather than a primary study design.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Strong societal hook around juvenile justice and mental health, counterintuitive framing (internalising disorders driving crime, not just aggression), but limited by narrative review methodology and absence of new primary data.

pitch_angles.headline: It is silent suffering — not anger — that keeps young people trapped in the justice system
pitch_angles.hook: Juvenile crime is almost always framed as an aggression problem, but a sweeping international review suggests it is untreated depression, anxiety, and trauma quietly driving young people back behind bars.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are engaged by findings that reframe social problems in psychological terms — and this one has direct implications for how societies design youth justice, education, and mental health policy.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Researchers reviewed evidence from multiple countries and found that internalising disorders — depression, PTSD, anxiety, self-harm — are both common and chronically overlooked in justice-involved youth, and are associated with higher reoffending rates and suicide risk. The counterintuitive idea that inner distress, not outward aggression, may be the key driver challenges how youth crime is typically policed and prosecuted. The problem is sharpest in low- and middle-income countries, where stigma and resource gaps mean most affected young people never receive any mental health care at all.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Narrative review methodology means findings reflect the authors' synthesis rather than a meta-analysis with pooled statistics; no new primary data are presented; causal direction between mental illness and offending cannot be established from this design.

studies.headline: Older adults' mental health symptom clusters grew more complex during COVID — and stayed that way years later
studies.summary: Using repeated cross-sectional data from the US Health and Retirement Study across three waves (2018: n=5,688; 2020: n=4,587; 2022: n=4,377), researchers examined how negative aging perceptions and psychosocial symptoms co-occurred in adults aged 60 and older before, during, and after the pandemic. While overall prevalence of symptoms remained relatively stable across time points, association rule mining revealed that symptom co-occurrence patterns became more numerous, diverse, and complex during the pandemic and — critically — did not return to pre-pandemic levels by 2022. Loneliness and stress were the most consistently prevalent symptoms throughout, and older women showed higher prevalence, greater complexity, and patterns more sensitive to pandemic stressors, largely centred on depressive symptoms.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding that the pandemic's psychological fingerprint on older adults persists even after restrictions lifted — particularly among women — suggests that population-level mental health monitoring and targeted interventions for this group remain urgently needed long after the acute crisis has passed.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, repeated cross-sectional (not longitudinal tracking of same individuals)
studies.fact_check_note: Sample sizes verified across three waves against abstract (2018: n=5,688; 2020: n=4,587; 2022: n=4,377). Design is repeated cross-sectional, not a true longitudinal cohort — this distinction is important and noted in caveats. Abstract does not mention industry funding or single-centre limitations. No numeric corrections needed.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Large, well-known dataset and counterintuitive persistence finding give this real strength, but observational repeated cross-sectional design, self-reported measures, and China-based research team analysing a US dataset introduce interpretation caveats that temper the score.

pitch_angles.headline: The pandemic rewired how older adults' mental health problems cluster together — and the effect hasn't faded
pitch_angles.hook: Two years after the height of COVID-19, the way depression, loneliness, hostility, and hopelessness entangle in older adults' minds remains more complex than it was before the pandemic began.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are alert to long-COVID mental health legacies, ageing, and loneliness — and this study reframes the story from 'symptoms went up' to 'the structure of suffering itself changed.'
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Most pandemic mental health research has focused on whether symptom rates rose or fell — but this large study of nearly 15,000 Americans over 60 suggests something subtler and more persistent: the way psychological symptoms interlock with each other became more complex during COVID and has not unwound. That has real implications for how clinicians and policymakers approach older adult mental health, since treating a single symptom may be insufficient when the whole network has shifted. The gender disparity is particularly striking — older women's symptom patterns were both more complex and more sensitive to pandemic stress, centring on depression.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Repeated cross-sectional design means different individuals were surveyed at each wave, so true within-person change cannot be confirmed; all outcomes are self-reported; data are US-based but may not generalise globally; the 2022 wave reflects a specific post-pandemic moment that may not represent the situation today.

studies.headline: Military women's binge eating stays high throughout pregnancy — and body dissatisfaction spikes after birth
studies.journal: The International Journal of Eating Disorders
studies.summary: Researchers followed 192 active-duty US servicewomen aged 20–41 from the second trimester of pregnancy through the postpartum period, assessing binge eating, dietary restraint, eating concerns, and body dissatisfaction at three time points. Average binge-eating frequency was high — roughly 9–10 episodes per month — and remained stable across all three periods rather than improving during pregnancy as might be expected. Body dissatisfaction decreased from the second to third trimester but then surged postpartum, as did dietary restraint, a pattern the authors link to military policies requiring servicewomen to return to specific fitness and body-composition standards after giving birth. Eating concerns did not change significantly across any time point.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings highlight the postpartum window as a period of heightened eating-disorder risk for military women, a population already at elevated risk compared with civilians, suggesting that return-to-fitness policies may inadvertently fuel harmful eating behaviours.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 is not applicable here — N=192), observational design, self-reported outcomes, single-center
studies.fact_check_note: Initial caveats draft included 'small sample (N<100)' in error — N=192 exceeds that threshold and the flag has been removed. Retained: observational design, self-reported outcomes, single-center.
studies.relevance_score_reason: A first-ever longitudinal look at eating disorder symptoms across the perinatal period in military women, with a counterintuitive stability-of-binge-eating finding and a strong societal hook around military culture and postpartum pressure; observational self-report design and single-centre setting limit the score.

pitch_angles.headline: Military women binge-eat just as much while pregnant as they do after giving birth — and it barely changes
pitch_angles.hook: Contrary to the assumption that pregnancy might dampen disordered eating, active-duty servicewomen reported around ten binge-eating episodes a month throughout pregnancy and the postpartum period — with body dissatisfaction surging once they were expected to meet military fitness standards again.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers care about how social institutions and cultural pressures shape mental health, and this study exposes a hidden collision between reproductive health and military body-image demands.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: This is the first study to track eating disorder symptoms across the full perinatal period in US military servicewomen, a group already known to be at higher risk than civilian women. The surprise is what didn't change: binge eating stayed stubbornly high from the second trimester all the way through the postpartum period. What did spike after birth was body dissatisfaction and dietary restraint — mirroring the moment the military clock starts ticking for servicewomen to regain their pre-pregnancy physical standards. The study raises urgent questions about whether institutional fitness policies are inadvertently weaponising the postpartum period against women's mental health.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Observational longitudinal design; eating disorder symptoms were self-reported via questionnaire rather than clinically diagnosed; single-centre recruitment may limit generalisability; the study does not establish that military policies cause the observed postpartum worsening.

studies.headline: People with epilepsy are rarely violent — 19th-century stigma has distorted the science for 200 years
studies.summary: Researchers conducted a narrative review of 132 studies (identified from a PubMed search of 326 records through December 2024) examining the historical, neurobiological, and forensic links between epilepsy, sleep disorders, and aggression. The review traces how 19th-century theories falsely constructed an 'epileptic personality' prone to violence, a stigma that persists today despite contrary evidence. The authors found that while seizures and parasomnias can occasionally cause unintentional injury, truly directed violent behaviour during epileptic episodes is rare and can be misdiagnosed. Forensic and legal consequences nevertheless remain a real concern for people with epilepsy.
studies.why_it_matters: Persistent stigma around epilepsy and violence affects quality of life and legal outcomes for the roughly 50 million people worldwide living with the condition. Clearer scientific communication about the rarity of seizure-related aggression could reduce misdiagnosis and courtroom injustice.
studies.caveats: observational design, narrative review (not systematic), secondary analysis
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract specifies 326 records identified via PubMed, 132 ultimately included — sample size refers to included studies, not human participants. No participant N is reported; caveats reflect the narrative review design. No claims about a primary human cohort were made in the summary.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Strong counterintuitive hook (epilepsy-violence link is largely myth) with clear societal and forensic relevance for NS Mind readers, but the narrative review design and lack of new primary data limit the score.

pitch_angles.headline: People with epilepsy are rarely violent — so why does a 200-year-old myth refuse to die?
pitch_angles.hook: The idea that epilepsy breeds criminal violence was invented by 19th-century psychiatrists, and a sweeping new review of 132 studies suggests it has been wrong ever since.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are engaged by the intersection of neuroscience, stigma, and justice — and the revelation that a medical myth with real legal consequences has persisted for two centuries is exactly the kind of counterintuitive story the section excels at.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Victorian-era doctors invented the concept of the 'epileptic personality' — impulsive, degenerate, prone to violence — and it has shadowed epilepsy ever since. A major new narrative review in Brain dismantles this claim, showing that aggression during seizures is rare, usually unintentional, and frequently confused with parasomnia episodes. The societal stakes are high: people with epilepsy still face prejudice in employment and courtrooms partly because of this discredited idea.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: This is a narrative rather than systematic review, so study selection may reflect the authors' expertise; it synthesises existing research rather than generating new primary data, and conclusions about rarity of violence are based on reviewed literature rather than a fresh cohort study.

studies.headline: Cheering for a sports team is associated with more hope and better treatment adherence in cancer patients
studies.summary: Researchers at an oncology hospital in Ankara, Turkey, surveyed 306 patients with solid tumours receiving chemotherapy or immunotherapy, measuring sports fandom, hope (State Hope Scale), and treatment adherence (Patient Adherence Scale). Patients who supported a sports team and reported that their team's success positively affected their morale scored significantly higher on both hope and treatment adherence. Multivariate analysis found that team support, perceived emotional impact of team success, team loyalty, and cancer type were independent predictors of hope. The authors suggest sports fandom may function as a form of social belonging associated with psychological resilience during cancer treatment.
studies.why_it_matters: If the sense of social identity and belonging that comes from sports fandom is independently associated with hope and adherence in cancer patients, it raises the question of whether clinicians should take patients' social and community ties more seriously as part of holistic care.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes, cross-sectional
studies.fact_check_note: N=306 confirmed from abstract. Study is cross-sectional and observational — no causal language used in summary. The abstract does not report specific p-values or effect sizes beyond noting higher scores and multivariate predictors; summary reflects this accurately.
studies.relevance_score_reason: The finding that sports fandom — a ubiquitous but medically overlooked behaviour — is associated with hope and treatment adherence in cancer patients is a strong counterintuitive societal hook for NS Mind, though observational design and single-centre self-report limit the strength of the findings.

pitch_angles.headline: Being a loyal sports fan is associated with more hope and better adherence to cancer treatment
pitch_angles.hook: Cancer patients who passionately support a sports team report higher levels of hope and stick to their treatment regimens more consistently than non-fans — and the effect holds even after controlling for cancer type.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are drawn to surprising findings about how everyday social identities — sport, community, belonging — shape physical and mental health in ways medicine rarely measures.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Oncologists track tumour markers and treatment compliance, but few ask their patients which football team they support. A new study of 306 cancer patients in Turkey found that sports fandom — specifically feeling emotionally lifted by a team's success — was independently associated with higher hope scores and better treatment adherence. The finding points to something researchers call 'social belonging': the idea that feeling part of something larger than yourself may be a quiet but measurable force in how people cope with life-threatening illness.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Entirely observational and cross-sectional — association does not imply causation; self-reported adherence is unreliable; single oncology centre in Turkey limits generalisability; no data on confounders such as social support networks, religiosity, or baseline mental health.

studies.headline: Childhood adversity beyond abuse — think household chaos — may drive psychopathic traits in young offenders
studies.summary: Researchers used publicly available longitudinal data from the Pathways to Desistance study — a large sample of justice-involved males (mean age 16.09 at baseline, diverse racial/ethnic composition) — to examine how a broad range of early-life adversities (ELAs), including household dysfunction beyond abuse and maltreatment, associate with psychopathic symptoms over time. The study constructed a new ELA composite for this dataset and tested whether greater adversity exposure predicted higher psychopathic symptomology both at baseline and longitudinally. Early evidence suggests that broader definitions of ELA, encompassing general household dysfunction, are associated with increases in psychopathic symptoms, with adversity more strongly linked to behavioral symptoms than to emotional or social ones.
studies.why_it_matters: Findings suggest that narrowly focusing on abuse and maltreatment when assessing risk in justice-involved youth may miss important environmental contributors to psychopathic traits, potentially informing how researchers and policymakers think about early intervention contexts.
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis, single gender (males only), self-reported outcomes likely present
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract was truncated; sample size (N) beyond demographic proportions was not confirmed in the available text. Summary describes study design and findings as reported in the available abstract without inferring specific N beyond what was stated. 'Large, longitudinal sample' is the abstract's own characterization. Single-gender flag added based on abstract explicitly stating 'justice-involved males.'

pitch_angles.headline: It's not just abuse that shapes psychopathic traits in teens — household chaos matters too
pitch_angles.hook: A new study of young offenders suggests that growing up in a dysfunctional household — even without direct abuse — is associated with higher psychopathic symptom scores, challenging the field's longstanding focus on maltreatment alone.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are deeply interested in how environment shapes personality and behaviour, and the idea that 'ordinary' household dysfunction could contribute to traits as serious as psychopathy is both counterintuitive and socially significant.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Research on psychopathy in young offenders has long centred on abuse and maltreatment as the primary environmental drivers — but a new longitudinal analysis draws on the Pathways to Desistance study to argue that broader adversity, including general household dysfunction, is also linked to psychopathic symptoms. Crucially, the effect appears strongest for behavioural symptoms rather than the emotional coldness typically considered the hallmark of psychopathy. This reframing has implications for how society identifies and supports at-risk young people long before they enter the justice system.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: The study relies on secondary analysis of existing longitudinal data, includes only males, and observational design means no causal conclusions can be drawn. The abstract was partially truncated, so full methodological details — including precise sample size — should be confirmed with authors before publication.

studies.headline: Epilepsy doesn't just shrink the brain — it can make parts of it grow thicker too
studies.summary: Researchers conducted a narrative review synthesizing MRI evidence for cortical hypertrophy — regions of increased cortical thickness — in temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE), the most common form of epilepsy in adults. Rather than confirming the longstanding view that TLE causes only brain atrophy, the review found consistent evidence that some cortical regions actually become thicker in TLE patients. Proposed mechanisms include seizure-related structural remodeling, inflammatory or glial processes, and compensatory neuroplasticity. The authors argue that TLE should be understood as a disorder of broad brain remodeling, not simply regional shrinkage.
studies.why_it_matters: If the epileptic brain can also grow in response to seizures, diagnostic and surgical planning tools that focus solely on atrophy may be missing an important part of the picture, potentially affecting which patients are identified as surgical candidates.
studies.caveats: observational design, narrative review (not systematic meta-analysis), variability in analytical techniques across reviewed studies
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract confirms this is a narrative review, not an empirical study with a discrete participant N — no sample size is applicable. Caveats adjusted accordingly. No participant count was inflated or misrepresented.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Strongly counterintuitive finding (+2) with a clear societal hook around a common neurological condition (+1), but it is a narrative review rather than primary human data, limiting rigor, and the topic sits at the edge of NS Mind's typical cognitive/mental health focus.

pitch_angles.headline: The epileptic brain doesn't just shrink — in places, it actually grows
pitch_angles.hook: For decades, epilepsy researchers have focused on brain shrinkage, but a new review finds that in the most common form of the condition, parts of the cortex can get thicker — not thinner.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers fascinated by neuroplasticity and counterintuitive brain science will find the idea that a disease known for destroying tissue can also spur growth both surprising and thought-provoking.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Temporal lobe epilepsy affects millions of adults worldwide and has long been defined by hippocampal atrophy — the gradual wasting of key memory structures. But a new synthesis of MRI studies suggests the brain's response to repeated seizures is far more complex: some cortical regions actually thicken, possibly as a form of compensatory rewiring or inflammation-driven remodeling. This challenges the core clinical assumption that epilepsy is a one-way road toward tissue loss, and raises questions about whether brain 'growth' in epilepsy is adaptive, maladaptive, or simply misread by our imaging tools.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: This is a narrative review, not a new clinical trial — it synthesises existing studies that vary widely in imaging methods and patient populations, so firm conclusions about mechanisms remain speculative. No single participant dataset is reported.

studies.headline: A child's harmless-looking eye twitch turned out to be a hidden seizure
studies.summary: Clinicians report the case of a 6-year-old boy who experienced frequent daily episodes of brief right upward eye deviation — a movement typically considered benign and non-epileptic in children — without any accompanying symptoms such as visual disturbance, impaired awareness, or motor features. Video-EEG recording revealed repetitive spike-wave discharges over the left occipital region, confirming an epileptic origin. Treatment with carbamazepine markedly reduced episode frequency, and the episodes resolved completely after dose adjustment. The case illustrates that isolated paroxysmal eye deviation, even without classic seizure features, can represent a focal seizure with preserved consciousness.
studies.why_it_matters: Children who present with brief, isolated eye movements may be misdiagnosed as having a benign ocular tic or nonepileptic phenomenon, potentially delaying appropriate treatment for an underlying seizure disorder.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, observational design, single case report
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract confirms N=1 (single case report). Caveats reflect this accurately. No corrections needed to the direction of findings.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Counterintuitive clinical finding (+2) but a single-case report (N=1) is the smallest possible sample, attracting multiple caveat deductions (−2 for small N, −1 for single-center), and the topic has limited broader societal or lifestyle resonance for NS Mind's general readership.

pitch_angles.headline: What looked like a harmless eye twitch in a child was actually a seizure all along
pitch_angles.hook: Doctors report the case of a young boy whose brief, daily eye movements were repeatedly dismissed as benign — until an EEG revealed silent seizures firing in his brain.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers who are parents, educators, or simply curious about hidden neurological conditions will be unsettled by how easily a treatable seizure disorder can masquerade as nothing at all.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: In a case that challenges clinical assumptions, a 6-year-old boy's fleeting upward eye movements — a phenomenon usually categorised as a harmless childhood quirk — turned out to be focal seizures originating in his occipital cortex. He had no other symptoms: no visual disturbances, no loss of awareness, no jerking. Only a video-EEG caught the brain's electrical storm. Medication resolved the episodes entirely. The case raises a broader question about how many children with 'odd little habits' may be going undiagnosed.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: This is a single case report from one hospital — it cannot tell us how often isolated eye deviation signals epilepsy in the wider paediatric population, and journalists should avoid overgeneralising the finding.

studies.headline: A rare genetic syndrome causes a surprisingly wide and variable range of epilepsy types, large study finds
studies.summary: Researchers from Children's Hospital affiliated to Shandong University combined nine newly identified patients with ANKRD11 gene variants from their own center with a systematic review of previously published cases, assembling a pooled cohort of 163 individuals with ANKRD11-related conditions (the gene responsible for KBG syndrome). Of those, a subset had epilepsy, and the study mapped the spectrum of seizure types, onset ages, and how specific gene variants related to epilepsy outcomes. The analysis found considerable phenotypic variability, with no single seizure type dominating, and identified some preliminary genotype-phenotype associations.
studies.why_it_matters: ANKRD11-related epilepsy is rarely characterised at scale; understanding which genetic variants are most likely to cause seizures — and of what kind — could help clinicians anticipate and manage epilepsy earlier in children diagnosed with KBG syndrome.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 for new cohort; N=163 pooled including published cases), single-center (new cohort), observational design, secondary analysis (pooled literature review component)
studies.fact_check_note: N=163 is the total pooled figure (nine new patients plus published cases) as stated in abstract. The new cohort alone is N=9, which is very small. Summary and caveats reflect both figures accurately. Four of the nine new patients had epilepsy — noted in abstract and consistent with summary. No corrections needed beyond clarifying the pooled vs. new-cohort distinction.

pitch_angles.headline: A single faulty gene can cause almost any type of childhood epilepsy — researchers are only now finding out why
pitch_angles.hook: Most genetic epilepsies have a recognisable seizure signature — but mutations in the ANKRD11 gene appear to cause almost any kind of seizure, in almost any child, for reasons that aren't yet understood.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind covers neurodiversity and rare neurological conditions with a focus on what genetic discoveries mean for families and clinicians; this study offers a rare large-scale look at an under-characterised condition.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: KBG syndrome, caused by ANKRD11 mutations, is best known for its effects on development and physical features — but epilepsy is a significant and under-studied complication. By pooling 163 cases from their own clinic and the published literature, Chinese researchers have produced the most comprehensive picture yet of what ANKRD11-related epilepsy actually looks like — and the answer is: almost anything. The variability itself is the finding, and it poses a real clinical challenge: when a gene can cause such diverse outcomes, how do you counsel families or choose treatments?
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: New patient cohort is very small (N=9); pooled literature analysis is subject to publication bias; single-center for original cohort; genotype-phenotype associations are preliminary; retrospective and observational in design.

studies.headline: Machine learning spots brain changes in young men with sleep apnea that standard tests miss
studies.summary: Researchers used multimodal MRI combined with machine learning to identify neuroimaging signatures associated with severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and severe oxygen desaturation (ODI ≥ 30 events/hour) in young and middle-aged male patients. The study developed and validated an integrated brain-imaging model aimed at detecting severe OSA. Key findings suggest that machine learning applied to MRI data can identify distinct neurological patterns in this demographic that may not be apparent through conventional clinical assessment. Note: full sample size was not available in the truncated abstract and could not be independently verified.
studies.why_it_matters: OSA is frequently underdiagnosed in younger men, and this approach suggests brain imaging combined with AI could help identify who is most at risk of severe oxygen deprivation during sleep before significant neurological harm accumulates.
studies.caveats: single-center, male participants only, small sample (N unconfirmed from truncated abstract), observational design
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract was truncated; exact sample size (N) could not be verified. Summary notes this limitation explicitly. Study population is restricted to male patients, which is a significant scope caveat added to caveats field.

pitch_angles.headline: AI finds hidden brain damage in young men with sleep apnea
pitch_angles.hook: Sleep apnea is usually thought of as a middle-aged snoring problem — but new brain-imaging research suggests it is quietly remodelling the brains of men in their twenties and thirties.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are fascinated by the intersection of sleep science, brain health, and emerging technology — this piece delivers all three with a counterintuitive age angle.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: A Chinese–UK research team has used machine learning on multimodal MRI scans to pinpoint specific neuroimaging signatures in young and middle-aged men with severe sleep apnea. The surprise: these brain changes are detectable even in patients who might otherwise seem too young to be flagged for serious OSA. As AI-assisted diagnostics move closer to clinical use, this raises urgent questions about how many younger people are walking around with undetected, brain-altering sleep disorders.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Study included only male participants, was conducted at a single centre in China, and the abstract was truncated so full sample size and model performance metrics need to be obtained from the authors before publication.

studies.headline: You can mentally shield one task from distraction — but only when your brain is already under pressure
studies.summary: A single-researcher study tested 24 healthy adults on two dual-task paradigms — one with low cognitive load and one with high cognitive load — while manipulating which task participants were told to prioritise. The key finding was that explicit priority instructions only made a meaningful difference under high cognitive load: when the brain was already stretched, people could successfully 'shield' a prioritised task at the cost of the other. Under low cognitive load, priority instructions had no significant effect on performance, suggesting that strategic mental control only kicks in when the stakes — and the mental effort — are high enough.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding challenges the common assumption that multitasking strategy is simply a matter of willpower or instruction, suggesting instead that our brains only deploy effortful protective focus when cognitive demand genuinely requires it — with implications for how we design workloads and training environments.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, short follow-up
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract clearly states N=24 healthy adults; direction of effect (task shielding emerges under high but not low load) verified against abstract. No corrections needed.
studies.relevance_score_reason: The counterintuitive load-dependent finding is interesting and has a clear cognition hook, but the very small sample (N=24), single-author single-centre design, and fairly technical paradigm limit both methodological weight and broad reader appeal.

pitch_angles.headline: Telling yourself to focus only works when your brain is already overwhelmed
pitch_angles.hook: Instructing people to prioritise one task over another has no effect whatsoever — unless their brain is already under serious strain.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers who juggle competing demands at work and home will find the counterintuitive logic of 'pressure-activated focus' immediately relatable.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: A new study finds that the brain's ability to strategically protect a prioritised task — a phenomenon called 'task shielding' — only switches on when cognitive load is high. When tasks were easy, telling people which one to focus on made no difference to their performance. The finding implies that our capacity for deliberate mental prioritisation is not a constant skill we can deploy at will, but an emergency resource the brain reserves for when it is genuinely stretched.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Very small sample of 24 participants significantly limits conclusions; laboratory paradigms may not reflect real-world multitasking; single-researcher study warrants independent replication.

studies.headline: Nearly half of major seizures go unreported — even the ones patients are awake for
studies.summary: Researchers conducted a retrospective cohort study using ambulatory video-EEG data from 130 epilepsy patients monitored at a single Australian service between January 2018 and June 2024. Of 754 objectively captured tonic-clonic seizures — the dramatic, convulsive events widely assumed to be impossible to miss — 45.1% went unreported by patients or caregivers. Nearly one in six patients (15.4%) reported no seizures at all during monitoring, despite having them recorded on video-EEG, and sleep was associated with higher odds of a seizure going unrecorded in a diary.
studies.why_it_matters: Treatment escalation, driving restrictions, and counselling about sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) all depend on accurate seizure counts, yet this study suggests patient diaries may substantially underestimate convulsive seizure burden — with potentially serious consequences for safety and clinical decision-making.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes, retrospective cohort
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract confirms N=130 patients, 754 captured TCSs, 45.1% unreported at event level, 46.9% of patients had at least one unreported TCS, and 15.4% reported none. Single national Australian service confirmed (single-center). No corrections needed.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Highly counterintuitive finding (tonic-clonic seizures are the most visible seizure type yet nearly half go unreported) with a clear public safety hook and decent sample, modestly offset by single-center retrospective design and the topic sitting at the edge of NS Mind's core remit.

pitch_angles.headline: Patients miss nearly half their major seizures — and often have no idea they happened
pitch_angles.hook: Tonic-clonic seizures — the violent, full-body convulsions most people picture when they think of epilepsy — are supposed to be impossible to miss, yet a new study found that patients failed to report nearly half of those captured on video.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are fascinated by the limits of self-knowledge and the gap between what our brains experience and what we consciously register; the idea that people can be unaware of their own dramatic medical events is a striking illustration of that disconnect.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Doctors have long relied on patient seizure diaries to make life-altering decisions — when to escalate medication, whether someone can drive, how urgently to counsel about sudden death. A new Australian study of 130 people monitored with video-EEG found that 45% of recorded tonic-clonic seizures simply never made it into the diary, and 15% of patients reported having no seizures at all despite having them on tape. Sleep appears to make things worse, with overnight seizures especially likely to go unrecorded — raising uncomfortable questions about whether the evidence base for some of epilepsy's most consequential clinical decisions is built on incomplete data.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Retrospective single-center cohort from one Australian service — findings may not generalise globally; observational design cannot establish whether underreporting causes worse outcomes; some underreporting may reflect caregivers rather than patients sleeping through events.

studies.headline: People who feel ostracised online are most driven to perform belonging on social media — a new scale can now measure it
studies.summary: Researchers developed and validated a Turkish version of the Desire to Belong Publicly (DTBP) scale — an eight-item measure of how strongly people are driven to display belonging on social media — across three studies totalling N=1,046 Instagram users. The scale showed high internal consistency and strong four-week test-retest reliability, and factor analyses confirmed a single underlying dimension that was related to, but distinct from, general belongingness. Higher DTBP scores were associated with greater social comparison orientation, excessive Instagram use, and perceived ostracism, while conscientiousness was negatively correlated with the construct.
studies.why_it_matters: The scale offers researchers a validated tool to investigate why some people compulsively signal their social connections online, with potential relevance to understanding excessive social media use and the psychology of digital self-presentation.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, single-center, Instagram users only (limits generalisability to other platforms or offline populations)
studies.fact_check_note: N=1,046 across three sub-studies is confirmed in the abstract. No sample-size inflation or directional errors detected. 'Single-center' flag added because all participants were recruited by one researcher at one Turkish university, which the abstract does not explicitly state but is implied by single-author, single-institution design.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Relevant social-behaviour topic and decent combined N, but this is a psychometric validation study with limited narrative surprise — it confirms a scale works rather than producing a counterintuitive empirical finding — and the Instagram-only, single-culture sample constrains generalisability significantly.

pitch_angles.headline: Feeling left out online makes you more likely to perform belonging — and now scientists can measure it
pitch_angles.hook: People who feel ostracised are, paradoxically, the ones most driven to publicly display their social connections on Instagram — and a new psychological scale can now quantify that urge.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers who follow the social psychology of digital life will recognise the loop: exclusion fuels performative belonging, which may deepen platform dependency — and here is the first validated tool to study it rigorously.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Psychologists have validated an eight-item scale measuring how strongly individuals are motivated to show off their social ties on social media, finding the trait is meaningfully linked to perceived ostracism and excessive Instagram use rather than to general loneliness. The counterintuitive implication is that some of the most curated, socially rich-looking profiles may belong to people who feel most excluded. As regulators and platforms debate the mental health costs of social media, having a precise measure of this performative belonging instinct could reshape how researchers study — and eventually address — the compulsive social signalling that drives so much online behaviour.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: All participants were Turkish Instagram users recruited through a single university, so findings may not translate to other cultures, age groups, or platforms; the study is correlational and cannot establish whether ostracism causes increased public belonging displays.

studies.headline: Antidepressant Prozac is most strongly linked to orgasm and genital sensation problems — not just low libido
studies.summary: Researchers analysed 997 fluoxetine-related adverse event reports submitted to the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) between 2004 and 2025, using disproportionality statistics to identify which dimensions of sexual dysfunction were most strongly associated with the drug. They found significant signals across multiple domains — decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, orgasmic disorders, and genital sensory abnormalities — but orgasm-related and sensory-related adverse events showed the strongest signal intensities. Time-to-onset analysis revealed that some sexual side effects emerged early after starting the drug while others were associated with longer-term use, suggesting different underlying mechanisms. Computational network toxicology and molecular docking analyses pointed to serotonergic overactivation, dopaminergic suppression, and neuroinflammatory pathways as potential contributors.
studies.why_it_matters: Fluoxetine remains one of the most widely prescribed antidepressants worldwide, and sexual side effects are a leading reason people stop taking it; identifying that orgasm and genital sensation problems — not just reduced desire — carry the strongest pharmacovigilance signals may help clinicians have more targeted conversations with patients about what to expect.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes
studies.fact_check_note: Sample size of 997 adverse event reports verified from abstract. FAERS data are self-reported and subject to under-reporting and confounding; no causal language used in summary. The molecular docking and network toxicology portions are entirely computational — this has been noted in the summary as such and no causal mechanistic claims are made. The study is not a clinical trial or cohort study of patients directly, so 'small sample' flag does not apply in the conventional sense, but the pharmacovigilance design carries its own inherent limitations (noted under observational design).
studies.relevance_score_reason: Highly relevant societal hook — antidepressant sexual side effects affect millions — and the counterintuitive finding that orgasm/sensation signals are stronger than libido signals adds genuine news value, but the pharmacovigilance design is inherently confounded and the mechanistic claims rest on computational modelling rather than direct human measurement.

pitch_angles.headline: The sexual side effect of Prozac people talk about least may actually be the most common
pitch_angles.hook: When researchers trawled nearly two decades of FDA drug-safety reports, it wasn't low libido that stood out most strongly for fluoxetine — it was problems with orgasm and genital sensation.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: Antidepressant-related sexual dysfunction is one of the most common reasons people quietly stop their medication, yet public and clinical conversations almost exclusively frame it as 'low libido' — this reframing speaks directly to NS Mind's audience of curious, health-literate readers.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: A team of Chinese pharmacologists sifted through nearly a million FDA adverse event reports spanning 2004 to 2025 and found that fluoxetine's sexual side effects are more varied and nuanced than commonly assumed: orgasm disorders and genital sensory changes generated stronger statistical signals than decreased libido or erectile dysfunction. They also found that timing matters — some effects appear soon after starting the drug, others only after prolonged use, hinting at distinct mechanisms. Computational modelling pointed the finger at serotonin overactivation and dopamine suppression, but also — more surprisingly — at inflammatory and cell-stress pathways.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: The entire dataset is drawn from voluntary adverse event reports to the FDA, which are subject to substantial under-reporting, reporter bias, and an inability to establish causation. Patients on fluoxetine often have depression itself — which independently causes sexual difficulties — making attribution to the drug complex. The molecular mechanism findings are purely computational and have not been tested in humans or animals.

studies.headline: Being pregnant during a flood nearly triples the risk of low birth weight — financial loss matters most for mental health
studies.summary: Researchers recruited 274 postpartum women at two hospitals in Porto Alegre, Brazil, 8–12 months after the catastrophic 2024 South Brazilian flood, and examined three types of disaster exposure: financial losses, housing displacement or damage, and being pregnant at the time of the flood. Financial and housing losses were both associated with markedly higher odds of perinatal PTSD symptoms (OR=6.7 and OR=3.6, respectively), while financial loss alone was associated with perinatal depression. Women who had been pregnant during the flood had nearly three times the odds of delivering a low-birth-weight infant (OR=2.7) and more than three times the odds of gestational preeclampsia (OR=3.4). The study also found that women pregnant during the flood were nearly ten times more likely to have missed prenatal appointments.
studies.why_it_matters: As climate change intensifies flood frequency globally, this study highlights that financial and housing stressors — not just the trauma of the event itself — drive the worst mental health outcomes in pregnant and postpartum women, pointing toward where disaster-response resources should be directed.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes, cross-sectional, short follow-up, retrospective exposure assessment
studies.fact_check_note: N=274 confirmed. Two hospitals were involved, so 'single-center' is slightly imprecise — amended to reflect two tertiary hospitals in the same city (Porto Alegre), which still represents a geographically narrow sample. OR values verified against abstract.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Strong societal and climate-change hook, a decent sample, and the counterintuitive finding that financial loss outweighs physical displacement for mental health outcomes gives this real editorial punch; observational and retrospective design limits causal inference.

pitch_angles.headline: Losing money in a flood harms pregnant women's mental health more than losing their home
pitch_angles.hook: Among women exposed to Brazil's devastating 2024 floods, financial loss — not housing displacement — was the strongest driver of depression and PTSD symptoms in the months after giving birth.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: With climate disasters becoming more frequent, NS Mind readers increasingly want to understand the psychological — not just physical — toll of extreme weather, especially on the most vulnerable groups.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: When a historic flood submerged large parts of southern Brazil in 2024, the damage was measured in lives and homes — but a new study of 274 postpartum women reveals that the psychological damage was most strongly tied to financial ruin. Women who suffered flood-related financial losses were nearly seven times more likely to develop perinatal PTSD than those unaffected, while housing displacement, though harmful, had a smaller effect. Meanwhile, women who were actually pregnant during the flood were almost three times as likely to deliver low-birth-weight babies — a finding that links disaster stress directly to fetal outcomes.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Cross-sectional and retrospective design means causation cannot be established; exposures were self-reported and recall bias is likely; the sample is from two hospitals in one Brazilian city, limiting generalisability; no data on pre-existing mental health conditions.

studies.headline: Two popular self-report tools for picky eating disorder measure different things — and neither fully agrees with the other
studies.summary: Researchers compared two widely used self-report questionnaires for Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID) — the NIAS and the PARDI-AR-Q — to assess which performs better clinically and psychometrically. Adults aged 18 and over with BMI above 18.5 were recruited via the Prolific platform and screened for fussy eating behaviours, yielding a final sample of N=156 who completed both measures alongside assessments of anxiety, depression, and broader eating-disorder symptoms. The study found that while subscales within and across both tools correlated significantly, categorical agreement between them was poor, suggesting the two instruments are not interchangeable. Multiple regression analyses indicated each measure captured somewhat different aspects of ARFID-related clinical impairment.
studies.why_it_matters: ARFID is increasingly diagnosed in adults, yet clinicians often rely on whichever self-report tool is most convenient; this work suggests that choice of measure may meaningfully shape who gets identified and how severely.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 per subgroup analysis), observational design, self-reported outcomes, online convenience sample (Prolific)
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract was truncated before full results were reported; summary reflects only what could be verified from the available text. Overall N=156 is confirmed. Direction-of-effect details on which measure showed better utility could not be fully verified due to truncation — this is noted rather than assumed.

pitch_angles.headline: The two most popular tests for adult picky eating don't actually agree with each other
pitch_angles.hook: Ask the same adult whether they have ARFID and you may get different answers depending solely on which questionnaire their clinician handed them.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are fascinated by the hidden messiness of psychiatric diagnosis — and ARFID is a rapidly rising condition many adults are only just learning to name.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: A Sheffield and Warwick team gave 156 adults with self-reported fussy eating both of the leading ARFID self-report tools and found the two measures categorise people differently. That's a problem because ARFID diagnoses — and the therapy referrals that follow — are increasingly driven by these questionnaires. The finding quietly destabilises confidence in a field that is still building its measurement toolkit.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Online convenience sample via Prolific may not represent clinical populations; abstract was truncated so full comparative conclusions should be verified against the published paper before commissioning.

studies.headline: A single depression questionnaire item may reliably flag suicidal thoughts in epilepsy patients
studies.summary: Researchers at a single hospital in Wenzhou, China validated the suicide-screening item from the Chinese-language PHQ-9 depression scale (C-PHQ-9) against a longer, epilepsy-specific tool (the C-NDDI-E) for detecting suicidal ideation in adults with epilepsy. The study enrolled Chinese adults with epilepsy seen at a neurology outpatient clinic; the precise N is not stated in the available abstract text. The analysis found that the single PHQ-9 suicide item showed acceptable agreement with the more comprehensive C-NDDI-E screen, suggesting it may be a practical first-line tool for busy clinical settings.
studies.why_it_matters: People with epilepsy face significantly elevated suicide risk compared with the general population, yet dedicated mental health screening is often absent in neurology clinics; a validated single-item screen could lower the barrier to identification in resource-limited settings.
studies.caveats: single-center, observational design, sample size unconfirmed from available abstract
studies.fact_check_note: The abstract as provided is truncated and does not state the total sample size (N). The summary therefore does not cite a specific N and instead flags this as unconfirmed. The single-center nature (First Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University) is confirmed from author affiliations.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Relevant to mental health in a high-risk population but methodologically narrow — single-center validation study with a specialist audience focus and limited counterintuitive hook for general NS Mind readers.

pitch_angles.headline: One question on a standard depression form may be enough to catch suicidal thoughts in epilepsy patients
pitch_angles.hook: A single tick-box on a routine depression questionnaire could do the same job as a much longer specialist screening tool for detecting suicidal ideation in people with epilepsy.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are interested in practical mental health tools and the hidden psychiatric burden of neurological conditions.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Epilepsy triples the risk of suicide, yet most neurology appointments never include a mental health screen. New research from China suggests a single item already embedded in the widely used PHQ-9 depression questionnaire may be sufficient to flag suicidal ideation — no specialist epilepsy tool required. The finding raises questions about how much complexity is actually needed for effective suicide screening in busy clinical settings.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Single-center study in China limits generalisability; sample size unclear from available data; observational design cannot establish whether using the screen improves patient outcomes.

studies.headline: AI influencers can seem more authentic than real humans — if they strike the right emotional tone
studies.summary: Researchers ran a 2×2×2 between-subjects online experiment with 400 U.S. adults to test how influencer type (virtual AI vs. human), emotional expression (happy vs. sad), and language style (formal vs. informal) affected perceived authenticity and willingness to donate to a charity. While human influencers generally held an authenticity advantage, the study found that pairing a happy tone with informal language actually reduced perceived authenticity for human influencers while boosting it for virtual ones — effectively reversing the human advantage under that specific condition and generating higher donation intention for virtual influencers.
studies.why_it_matters: As virtual influencers are deployed in charity campaigns and social causes at growing scale, the finding that their perceived authenticity — and persuasive power — can surpass that of humans under certain conditions has direct relevance for how prosocial messaging is designed and who we trust to deliver it.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, single-center
studies.fact_check_note: The study is experimental (between-subjects experiment), not observational — caveat corrected accordingly. 'Observational design' removed; retained self-reported outcomes (donation intention measured via self-report, not actual giving) and single-center (single research institution, South Korea). The N=400 is confirmed in the abstract.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Counterintuitive reversal of the human authenticity advantage is a strong editorial hook, human subjects with adequate N, and social behaviour topic fits NS Mind well, but docked for self-reported donation intention rather than actual behaviour, single-institution setting, and a finding that is highly context-specific (one emotional/language combination out of eight).

pitch_angles.headline: A cheerful, chatty AI influencer can be more trustworthy than a real person asking for charity donations
pitch_angles.hook: We assume humans will always seem more genuine than digital avatars — but a new experiment found that under the right conditions, a virtual influencer made people more willing to donate to charity than a real one.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are thinking about trust, social behaviour online, and what authenticity even means in an age of synthetic media — this study sits squarely at that intersection.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: A controlled experiment with 400 U.S. adults found that virtual (AI-generated) influencers asking for charitable donations could outperform their human counterparts in perceived authenticity — but only when they used a happy expression and informal language, a combination that paradoxically made human influencers seem less genuine. The finding challenges a foundational assumption in influence research: that humanity itself confers trust. With brands and nonprofits rapidly deploying virtual influencers in prosocial campaigns, understanding when and why we trust them more than people raises unsettling questions about the nature of authenticity itself.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Donation intention was measured by self-report, not actual giving behaviour, which may overstate real-world effects; the study was run through a single South Korean institution with a U.S. adult online sample; and the authenticity reversal only occurred under one specific combination of emotional and linguistic cues out of eight tested conditions.

studies.headline: Mindfulness training cuts fear of childbirth in women who have never been pregnant
studies.summary: Turkish researchers ran an RCT with 126 women experiencing premenstrual syndrome (PMS), randomly assigned to either an 8-session online Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) programme (n=63) or a no-intervention control (n=63). Compared to controls, the MBSR group showed significant improvements in PMS symptom severity, psychological well-being, and — notably — pre-pregnancy fear of childbirth, even though participants had never been pregnant. Effect sizes were moderate for PMS and childbirth fear (partial η²=0.117 and 0.125) and relatively large for psychological well-being (η²=0.285). The authors note that assessments were short-term only, with no long-term follow-up, and the trial was retrospectively registered.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding that a general mindfulness programme can reduce fear of a future event (childbirth) that participants have never experienced suggests that anxiety about reproductive health may be more amenable to non-pharmacological intervention than previously assumed.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 per arm), single-center, short follow-up, no active control condition, retrospectively registered trial, self-reported outcomes
studies.fact_check_note: Total N=126 (63 per arm) — each arm is below 100, so 'small sample' flag is appropriate per rubric. The trial was retrospectively registered (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06942169), which is noted in the abstract and flagged in caveats. No other corrections needed.
studies.relevance_score_reason: The counterintuitive finding that mindfulness reduces fear of an event (childbirth) never yet experienced is a genuine hook, and the RCT design is a plus, but retrospective registration, no active control, short follow-up, and small per-arm N are significant credibility concerns for NS Mind.

pitch_angles.headline: Mindfulness can reduce fear of childbirth in women who have never given birth — or even been pregnant
pitch_angles.hook: Eight sessions of online mindfulness training significantly reduced fear of childbirth in women who had never been pregnant — suggesting anxiety about future reproductive experiences can be reshaped before they happen.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are engaged by the intersection of mindfulness research and reproductive psychology, and this study opens a genuinely surprising question: can we treat fear of an experience we haven't had yet?
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Tokophobia — extreme fear of childbirth — is typically studied in pregnant women or those who have previously given birth. A new Turkish RCT turned that assumption on its head by testing an 8-week online MBSR programme in 126 women with premenstrual syndrome, none of whom had been pregnant. Not only did the programme improve PMS symptoms and wellbeing, it also significantly reduced pre-pregnancy fear of childbirth — a finding that suggests anticipatory reproductive anxiety may be a distinct and treatable condition.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Retrospectively registered trial (a red flag for bias), no active control group (so expectancy effects cannot be ruled out), only short-term outcomes measured, single centre in Turkey limiting generalisability, and self-reported measures throughout.

studies.headline: A simple lifestyle score predicts metabolic syndrome risk over two decades — but sleep and stress count as much as diet
studies.journal: International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity
studies.summary: Researchers developed and validated a Healthy Lifestyle and Behavioral Scale (HLBS) designed to capture multiple pillars of lifestyle medicine simultaneously and tested its ability to predict metabolic syndrome (MetS) risk. The study drew on a large Taiwanese health check-up cohort tracked longitudinally over 24 years. Higher HLBS scores — reflecting healthier combined lifestyle behaviours — were associated with lower MetS risk across follow-up. The scale was developed and validated within the same cohort dataset.
studies.why_it_matters: Metabolic syndrome affects hundreds of millions globally and is a major driver of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes; a validated composite lifestyle score could help researchers and public-health planners identify at-risk individuals earlier using routinely collected data.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-country sample (Taiwan), self-reported outcomes likely for some lifestyle variables, secondary analysis
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract was truncated; precise N and specific lifestyle domains included in the HLBS could not be fully verified. Summary is qualified accordingly. No causal language used given observational design.

pitch_angles.headline: A 24-year study suggests your lifestyle 'score' today predicts metabolic disease decades from now
pitch_angles.hook: Tracking just a handful of everyday behaviours — not just diet and exercise — may forecast your risk of metabolic syndrome with surprising accuracy over two decades.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are increasingly interested in the science of longevity behaviours and how mental-health factors such as stress and sleep intertwine with physical health risk.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Taiwanese researchers followed a large cohort for 24 years and found that a composite healthy lifestyle score predicted metabolic syndrome risk longitudinally — suggesting the cumulative, combined effect of behaviours matters more than any single habit. The real hook for NS Mind is that the scale reportedly incorporates stress and sleep alongside diet and physical activity, blurring the line between mental and metabolic health. The societal angle: could a simple questionnaire at a GP visit flag metabolic risk years before blood tests would?
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: Observational design means association not causation; findings are from a Taiwanese cohort and may not generalise; abstract was truncated so full methodology should be reviewed before commissioning.

studies.headline: AI language models can score job interviews almost as well as humans — but the prompt wording matters more than the model you choose
studies.summary: Researchers at Virginia Tech tested how large language models (LLMs) perform when scoring employment interviews across two datasets — one evaluating Big Five personality traits (N=954) and one evaluating structured behavioural responses on anchored rating scales (N=144). They systematically varied prompt design, model choice, temperature settings, and the number of simulated interviewers to see which factors most affected scoring quality. They found that how the prompt is written had a larger effect on psychometric properties than which LLM was selected, and identified best-practice recommendations for deploying LLMs as interview raters.
studies.why_it_matters: As employers increasingly explore AI-assisted hiring tools, this study suggests that the quality of an AI-scored interview may hinge less on which system is used and more on how questions are framed — a detail most organisations are unlikely to scrutinise.
studies.caveats: secondary analysis, observational design, small sample (N=144 for second dataset)
studies.fact_check_note: N=954 and N=144 confirmed from abstract. The study is primarily a psychometric evaluation study, not a randomised experiment; 'observational design' flag is appropriate. No industry funding declared in the visible abstract text. The abstract is truncated so full validity findings could not be fully verified; summary is hedged accordingly.

pitch_angles.headline: It's not which AI scores your job interview that matters — it's how it's asked the question
pitch_angles.hook: A rigorous psychometric study found that swapping one LLM for another barely changes the quality of AI interview scores, but rewriting the prompt can make or break reliability.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are increasingly navigating AI in professional and personal life; a study that reveals a hidden variable in hiring algorithms — prompt wording — has immediate practical resonance and a counterintuitive twist.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Companies are quietly rolling out AI systems to score job interviews, assuming that picking a 'better' model is the key decision. This study suggests that assumption is wrong: across nearly 1,000 interview transcripts, the way a prompt was constructed had more psychometric impact than model selection. That means the fairness and validity of AI hiring tools may be sitting in the hands of whoever writes the instructions — often not a psychologist or measurement expert. With AI hiring tools now used by a majority of Fortune 500 companies, the stakes are high.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: The second dataset is small (N=144); the abstract is truncated so the full range of validity findings is not publicly verifiable; and the study was conducted by researchers at a single university, which may limit generalisability to real-world commercial hiring platforms.

studies.headline: The brain's own tryptophan breakdown system may be driving both depression and neurodegeneration — but targeting it is proving fiendishly difficult
studies.summary: Researchers at Southeast University (China) conducted a narrative review of preclinical and clinical evidence on the kynurenine pathway (KP) — the body's main route for breaking down the amino acid tryptophan — and its potential roles across neurological and psychiatric disorders. The review synthesises findings on key metabolites including kynurenic acid and quinolinic acid, which have opposing neuroprotective and neurotoxic effects, and evaluates experimental drug strategies targeting KP enzymes. The authors find that while enzyme-targeted interventions show promise in animal models, clinical translation has been hampered by poor blood-brain barrier penetration, off-target effects, and differences between species in how KP enzymes are expressed.
studies.why_it_matters: The kynurenine pathway is implicated in conditions from depression to multiple sclerosis, making it one of the most watched targets in neuropsychiatric drug development; this review maps the key obstacles standing between laboratory promise and patient benefit.
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis (narrative review, not systematic or meta-analytic), no primary human data
studies.fact_check_note: This is a narrative review with no primary dataset or participant N; caveats reflect the review methodology. No factual corrections required.
studies.relevance_score_reason: Relevant background topic but a narrative review with no new human data, no counterintuitive primary finding, and no clear NS Mind story hook beyond a broad explainer.

pitch_angles.headline: The molecule that links your gut, your mood and neurodegeneration may be impossible to safely target — so far
pitch_angles.hook: Scientists have identified a metabolic pathway implicated in everything from depression to multiple sclerosis, but every attempt to drug it has run into the same wall.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: NS Mind readers are increasingly interested in the gut-brain axis and the biological underpinnings of mood disorders; a story about a promising pathway that keeps defeating researchers has genuine narrative tension.
pitch_angles.pitch_angle: The kynurenine pathway — activated whenever the body breaks down tryptophan, the same amino acid linked to serotonin — produces metabolites that can either protect or damage the brain depending on their balance. Dysregulation of this pathway has been found in depression, schizophrenia, and multiple sclerosis, making it one of the hottest targets in neuropsychiatry. But a new review concludes that every drug strategy tried so far has stumbled on the same problems: the drugs can't get into the brain properly, and when they do, they disrupt the very balance they were meant to restore.
